Embeddings of Affine Spaces into Quadrics

Jérémy Blanc Address: Jérémy Blanc, Universität Basel, Departement Mathematik und Informatik, Spiegelgasse 11, CH-40514051 Basel, Switzerland Email address: jeremy.blanc@unibas.ch and Immanuel van Santen (né Stampfli) Address: Immanuel van Santen, Fachbereich Mathematik der Universität Hamburg, Bundesstraße 5555, DE-2014620146 Hamburg, Germany Email address: immanuel.van.santen@math.ch
Abstract.

This article provides, over any field, infinitely many algebraic embeddings of the affine spaces 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} into smooth quadrics of dimension two and three respectively, which are pairwise non-equivalent under automorphisms of the smooth quadric. Our main tools are the study of the birational morphism SL2→𝔸3\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{3} and the fibration SL2→𝔸3→𝔸1\mathrm{SL}_{2}\to\mathbb{A}^{3}\to\mathbb{A}^{1} obtained by projections, as well as degenerations of variables of polynomial rings, and families of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations.

1. Introduction

In the sequel we denote by k the ground field of our algebraic varieties. Given two affine algebraic varieties X,YX,Y, we say that two closed embeddings ρ,ρ′:X↪Y\rho,\rho^{\prime}\colon X\hookrightarrow Y are equivalent if there exists an automorphism φ∈Aut⁡(Y)\varphi\in\Aut(Y) such that ρ′=φ∘ρ\rho^{\prime}=\varphi\circ\rho. Similarly, we say that two closed subvarieties X,X′⊂YX,X^{\prime}\subset Y are equivalent if there exists an automorphism φ∈Aut⁡(Y)\varphi\in\Aut(Y) such that X′=φ⁡(X)X^{\prime}=\varphi(X). If two closed embeddings are equivalent, then their images are equivalent, but the converse is not always true and is related to the extension of automorphisms.

In the Bourbaki Seminar Challenging problems on affine nn-space [Kra96], Hanspeter Kraft gives a list of eight fundamental problems related to the affine nn-spaces. The third one is the following:

Embedding Problem. Is every closed embedding 𝔸km↪𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{m}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} equivalent to the standard embedding (x1,…,xm)↦(x1,…,xm,0,…,0)(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})\mapsto(x_{1},\dots,x_{m},0,\dots,0)?

This question, asked over the ground field k=ℂ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}=\mathbb{C} in [Kra96], has until now no negative answer. For k=ℝ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}=\mathbb{R}, it is easy to find counterexamples for m=1m=1 and n=3n=3, by taking embeddings which are not topologically trivial (non-trivial knots), see for instance the example of [Sha92], reproduced below in Example 6.1. In positive characteristic, there are counterexamples when m=n−1m=n-1 (see Proposition 3.16). The embedding problem has however a positive answer in the following cases:

  1. (1)

    m=1m=1, n=2n=2, char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})=0 (Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki Theorem) [AM75, Suz74], [vdE00, Theorem 2.3.5];

  2. (2)

    n≥2​m+2n\geq 2m+2, k infinite (Theorem of Kaliman, Nori and Srinivas [Kal91, Sri91]).

The case of hypersurfaces (m=n−1)(m=n-1) is of particular interest. In this case, the image is given by the zero set of an irreducible polynomial equation f∈k​[𝔸n]f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[{\mathbb{A}}^{n}]. One necessary condition for an embedding to be equivalent to the standard embedding consists of asking that the other fibres of f:𝔸kn→𝔸k1f\colon{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1} are affine spaces. In fact, for any field k and any n≥1n\geq 1, there is no known example of a hypersurface X⊂𝔸knX\subset{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{n} isomorphic to 𝔸kn−1{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{n-1} and given by f=0f=0, f∈k​[𝔸n]f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[{\mathbb{A}}^{n}] irreducible such that another fibre f=λf=\lambda is not isomorphic to 𝔸kn−1{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{n-1}. It is conjectured by Abhyankar and Sathaye that no such examples exist, at least when char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})=0, see [vdE00, §3, page 103], even if this is quite strong and seems “unlikely” (as Arno van den Essen says in [vdE00, §3, page 103]). Moreover, for n=3n=3 and char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})=0, the fact that infinitely many fibres f=λf=\lambda are isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} implies that the fibration is equivalent to the standard one, and in particular that all fibres are isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} [KZ01, Kal02, DK09]. For char⁡(k)>0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})>0, there is until now no known counterexample to the above conjecture, which is open even in dimension n=2n=2 (and corresponds to a question of Abhyankar, see [Gan11, Question 1.1]).

In this paper, we replace the affine space at the target by some analogue varieties, namely affine smooth quadrics. This simplifies the question in such a way that one can actually give an answer. Moreover, it also gives some idea on what kind of behaviour one could expect in a general situation.

In dimension n=2n=2, the most natural quadric is

Q2=Spec⁡(k​[x,y,z]/(x​y−z⁡(z+1)))⊂𝔸k3.Q_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y,z]/(xy-z(z+1)))\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

In fact, if k is an algebraically closed field, then every smooth quadric hypersurface Q⊂𝔸k3Q\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, (𝔸k1∖{0})×𝔸k1({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\})\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} or Q2Q_{2}, as one can see using the classification of quadratic forms. As all embeddings of 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} into (𝔸k1∖{0})×𝔸k1({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\})\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} are constant on the first factor, they are all equivalent. Over any field, the group of automorphisms of Q2Q_{2} is similar to the one of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, as it is an amalgamated product of two factors, corresponding to affine maps and triangular maps [BD11, Theorem 5.4.5(7)(a)]. This is also the case for the affine surface ℙk2∖Γ{\mathbb{P}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\Gamma, where Γ⊂ℙk2\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2} is any smooth conic having a k-point (see for instance [DD16, Theorem 2]). If char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})=0, there is exactly one (respectively two) closed curve C⊂𝔸k2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} (respectively C⊂ℙk2∖ΓC\subset{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma) isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, up to automorphism of the surface. This follows from the Abhyankar-Moh-Suzuki Theorem for 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} and from [DD16] for ℙk2∖Γ{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma. In particular, all automorphisms of the corresponding curves extend to automorphisms of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} or ℙk2∖Γ{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma. Similarly, a complex toric affine surface admits only finitely many embeddings of 𝔸ℂ1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbb{C}}, up to equivalence [AZ13]. By contrast, we prove the following result:

Theorem 1.

For each field k, there is an infinite set of closed curves

Ci⊂Q2=Spec⁡(k​[x,y,z]/(x​y−z⁡(z+1))),i∈I,C_{i}\subset Q_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y,z]/(xy-z(z+1))),\ i\in I,

which are pairwise non-equivalent up to automorphism of Q2Q_{2}, such that each CiC_{i} is isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} and such that the identity is the only automorphism of CC that extends to an automorphism of Q2Q_{2}. Moreover, if k is uncountable, then one can choose the same for II.

In dimension n=3n=3, the most natural quadric is

SL2=Spec⁡(k​[t,u,x,y]/(x​y−t​u−1))⊂𝔸k4.\SL_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(xy-tu-1))\subset{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{4}\,.

Similarly as in dimension two, over an algebraically closed field k, every quadric hypersurface in 𝔸k4{\mathbb{A}}^{4}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is isomorphic to 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, (𝔸k1∖{0})×𝔸k2({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\})\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, Q2×𝔸k1Q_{2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} or SL2\SL_{2}. Moreover, the quotient of SL2\SL_{2} by its maximal torus yields a morphism SL2→SL2/T≃Q2\SL_{2}\to\SL_{2}/T\simeq Q_{2}, which is the “universal torsor” (also called the Cox quotient presentation or the characteristic space), see [ADHL15, Examples 4.5.13–4.5.14].

We consider the quadric hypersurface SL2\SL_{2} more closely. Its automorphism group shares similar properties with the one of Aut⁡(𝔸k3)\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) (see [LV13, BFL14, Mar15]). Both are known to be complicate, as they contain “wild” automorphisms [LV13], and do not preserve any fibration, as it is the case for other varieties being topologically closer to 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, like the Koras-Russell threefold. However, in contrast to the quadric Q2Q_{2}, the quadric SL2\SL_{2} is closer to a contractible affine variety in the sense that the ring of regular functions on SL2\SL_{2} is a unique factorisation domain (see Lemma 4.4). The first difference concerning embeddings of affine spaces with the surfaces Q2,𝔸k2,ℙk2∖ΓQ_{2},{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}},{\mathbb{P}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\Gamma and with 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is that the “simplest embedding” 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} is more rigid in the following sense:

Theorem 2.

Let k be any field and let

ρ1:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(1ts1+s​t)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{1}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\ s&1+st\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

be the “standard” embedding. Then, an automorphism (s,t)↦(f⁡(s,t),g⁡(s,t))(s,t)\mapsto(f(s,t),g(s,t)) of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} extends to an automorphism of SL2\SL_{2}, via ρ1\rho_{1}, if and only if it has Jacobian determinant ∂f∂s​∂g∂t−∂f∂t​∂g∂s∈k∗\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\frac{\partial g}{\partial s}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} equal to ±1\pm 1. In particular, the following holds:

  1. (1)(1)

    every embedding 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} with image ρ1​(𝔸k2)\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) is equivalent to an embedding

    ρλ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(1tλ​s1+λ​s​t),\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{\lambda}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\ \lambda s&1+\lambda st\end{pmatrix},\end{array}

    for a certain λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast}. Moreover, ρλ\rho_{\lambda} and ρλ′\rho_{\lambda^{\prime}} are equivalent if and only if λ′=±λ\lambda^{\prime}=\pm\lambda;

  2. (2)(2)

    if k has at least 44 elements, then not all automorphisms of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} extend to SL2\SL_{2} via ρ1\rho_{1}.

Remark 1.1.

Let us make some comments on Theorem 2:

  1. (1)

    Over the field of complex numbers k=ℂ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}={\mathbb{C}}, we show that all algebraic automorphisms of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2} extend via the standard embedding ρ1\rho_{1} to holomorphic automorphisms of SL2\SL_{2}, see Remark 4.7.

  2. (2)

    If all component functions of a closed embedding f:𝔸k2↪SL2f\colon{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} are polynomials of degree ≤2\leq 2, then ff is equivalent to ρλ\rho_{\lambda} for a certain λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast} (Proposition 5.19).

Next, we focus on the closed embeddings 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} that are compatible with the simplest 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}-fibration of SL2\SL_{2}. More precisely:

Definition 1.2.

A closed embedding ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2\rho\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} is said to be a fibred embedding if it is of the form

ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(p⁡(s,t)tr⁡(s,t)q⁡(s,t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}p(s,t)&t\\ r(s,t)&q(s,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

for some p,q,r∈k​[s,t]p,q,r\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t]. This corresponds to the commutativity of the diagram

where π1:𝔸k2→𝔸k1\pi_{1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, π2:SL2→𝔸k1\pi_{2}\colon\SL_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} are respectively given by (s,t)↦t(s,t)\mapsto t and (xtuy)↦t\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto t.

As we will show, there are a lot of fibred embeddings (i.e. embeddings of the form (1.2)):

Theorem 3.

Let k be any field, let P∈k​[t,x,y]P\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] be a polynomial that is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y] ((which means that PP is the image of xx by some automorphism of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y])), and let HP⊂SL2=Spec⁡(k​[t,u,x,y]/(x​y−t​u−1))H_{P}\subset\SL_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(xy-tu-1)) and ZP⊂𝔸k3=Spec⁡(k​[t,x,y])Z_{P}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) be the hypersurfaces given by P=0P=0.

  1. (1)(1)

    The following conditions are equivalent:

    1. (a)(a)

      The hypersurface HP⊂SL2H_{P}\subset\SL_{2} is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

    2. (b)(b)

      The hypersurface HP⊂SL2H_{P}\subset\SL_{2} is the image of a fibred embedding 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}.

    3. (c)(c)

      The fibre of ZP→𝔸k1Z_{P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, (t,x,y)↦t(t,x,y)\mapsto t over every closed point of 𝔸k1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and the polynomial P​(0,x,y)∈k​[x,y]P(0,x,y)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] is of the form μ​xm​(x−λ)\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda) or μ​ym​(y−λ)\mu y^{m}(y-\lambda) for some μ,λ∈k∗\mu,\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and some m≥0m\geq 0.

  2. (2)(2)

    If P,Q∈k​[t,x,y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] are two polynomials of the above form satisfying the conditions (a)−(b)−(c)\eqref{ThmEqa}-\eqref{ThmEqb}-\eqref{ThmEqc}, such that HP,HQ⊂SL2H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2} are equivalent under an automorphism of SL2\SL_{2}, then ZP,ZQ⊂𝔸k3Z_{P},Z_{Q}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} are equivalent under an automorphism of 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

  3. (3)(3)

    There are infinitely many fibred embeddings 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} having pairwise non-equivalent images in SL2\SL_{2}. If k is uncountable, we can moreover choose uncountably many such embeddings.

Remark 1.3.

Let us make some comments on Theorem 3:

  1. (1)

    It is possible that HP,HQH_{P},H_{Q} are non-equivalent, even if ZP,ZQZ_{P},Z_{Q} are equivalent (Lemma 5.11).

  2. (2)

    If char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})=0, then every image of a fibred embedding 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} is of the form HPH_{P} as above (Lemma 5.2(2)). This is false if char⁡(k)>0\mathrm{char}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})>0 (Lemma 5.3).

Let us make the following comment concerning embeddings of 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} into the smooth quadric SL2\SL_{2} over the field k=ℂ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}={\mathbb{C}}. Although there are infinitely many non-equivalent embeddings of 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{{\mathbb{C}}} into SL2\SL_{2}, it is not known, whether all embeddings of 𝔸ℂ1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{C}}} into SL2\SL_{2} are equivalent under an algebraic automorphism. It seems that this questions is as difficult, as the question of non-equivalent embeddings 𝔸ℂ1↪𝔸ℂ3{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{C}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{{\mathbb{C}}}. However, up to holomorphic automorphisms, all embeddings of 𝔸ℂ1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{C}}} into 𝔸ℂ3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{{\mathbb{C}}} and into SL2\SL_{2} are equivalent, see [Kal92, Sta15].

In the last section (Lemma 6.2), we give an example of an embedding 𝔸ℝ1↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{R}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} which is non-equivalent to the standard embedding.

2. The smooth quadric of dimension 22 and the proof of Theorem 1

2.1. The isomorphism with the complement of the diagonal in ℙk1×ℙk1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}

In this section, we study the smooth quadric Q2⊂𝔸k3Q_{2}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by

Q2=Spec⁡(k​[x,y,z]/(x​y−z⁡(z+1))),Q_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y,z]/(xy-z(z+1))),

and more particularly closed embeddings 𝔸k1↪Q2{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow Q_{2}. Since the closure of Q2Q_{2} in ℙk3{\mathbb{P}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is a smooth quadric, isomorphic to ℙk1×ℙk1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, we get the following classical isomorphism:

Lemma 2.1.

The morphism

ρ:Q2→ℙk1×ℙk1(x,y,z)↦{([y:z],[z:x]) if ​z≠0([z+1:x],[y:z+1]) if ​z≠−1\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho\colon&Q_{2}&\to&{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\\ &(x,y,z)&\mapsto&\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}(&[y:z]&,&[z:x]&)&\text{ if }z\not=0\\ (&[z+1:x]&,&[y:z+1]&)&\text{ if }z\not=-1\end{array}\right.\end{array}

yields an isomorphism Q2⟶≃(ℙk1×ℙk1)∖ΔQ_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\setminus\Delta, where Δ⊂ℙk1×ℙk1\Delta\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is the diagonal, with an inverse given by

ψ:(ℙk1×ℙk1)∖Δ→Q2([u0:u1],[v0:v1])↦(u1​v1u0​v1−u1​v0,u0​v0u0​v1−u1​v0,u1​v0u0​v1−u1​v0)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\psi\colon&({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\setminus\Delta&\to&Q_{2}\\ &([u_{0}:u_{1}],[v_{0}:v_{1}])&\mapsto&\left(\frac{u_{1}v_{1}}{u_{0}v_{1}-u_{1}v_{0}},\frac{u_{0}v_{0}}{u_{0}v_{1}-u_{1}v_{0}},\frac{u_{1}v_{0}}{u_{0}v_{1}-u_{1}v_{0}}\right)\end{array}
Proof.

We first check that ρ⁡((,,,,,))∈(ℙk1×ℙk1)∖Δ\rho((x,y,z))\in({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\setminus\Delta for each (x,y,z)∈Q2(x,y,z)\in Q_{2}. If z≠0z\not=0 then [y:z]≠[z:x][y:z]\not=[z:x], since x​y−z2=z≠0xy-z^{2}=z\not=0. If z=0z=0, then x​y=0xy=0, whence [z+1:x]=[1:x]≠[y:1]=[y:z+1][z+1:x]=[1:x]\not=[y:1]=[y:z+1].

It remains then to check that ρ∘ψ=id(ℙk1×ℙk1)∖Δ\rho\circ\psi=\mathrm{id}_{({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\setminus\Delta} and ψ∘ρ=idQ2\psi\circ\rho=\mathrm{id}_{Q_{2}}, which follows from a straight-forward calculation. ∎

2.2. Families of embeddings

The following result is the key step in the proof of Theorem 1.

Lemma 2.2.

For each n≥1n\geq 1, let pn​(t)=tn​(t+1)n+1p_{n}(t)=t^{n}(t+1)^{n+1}. The closed curve Cn=νpn​(𝔸k1)⊂Q2C_{n}=\nu_{p_{n}}({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\subset Q_{2} is isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, via

Proof of Theorem 1.

If k is the field with two elements, then we conclude by Example 2.3. Hence we can assume that k contains more than two elements. 3. Variables of polynomial rings

In this section, we give some results on variables of polynomial rings. Most of them are classical or belong to the folklore. We include them for self-containedness and for lack of precise references.

Definition 3.1.

Let SS be a ring and let R⊂SR\subset S be a subring. We denote by AutR⁡(S)\Aut_{R}(S) the group of automorphisms of the RR-Algebra SS. More precisely,

AutR⁡(S)={ automorphism of rings ​f:S→S​ such that ​f|R=idR}.\Aut_{R}(S)=\left\{\text{ automorphism of rings }f\colon S\to S\text{ such that }f|_{R}=\mathrm{id}_{R}\right\}.
Definition 3.2.

Let RR be a domain and SS be a polynomial ring in n≥1n\geq 1 variables over RR, i.e. R⊂SR\subset S and there exist x1,…,xn∈Sx_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in S such that each element of SS can be written in a unique way as f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), where ff is a polynomial in the xix_{i} with coefficients in RR. An element v∈Sv\in S is called variable of the RR-algebra SS if there exists f∈AutR⁡(S)f\in\Aut_{R}(S) such that f⁡(v)=x1f(v)=x_{1}.

In the sequel, we often denote by R⁡[t]R[t] or R⁡[x]R[x] the polynomial ring in one variable over RR, by R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] the polynomial ring in two variables over RR and by R⁡[x1,…,xn]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] the polynomial ring in nn variables over RR.

Lemma 3.3.

Let RR be a domain, let S=R⁡[x1,…,xn]S=R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be the polynomial ring in nn variables over RR and let v∈Sv\in S. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)(1)

    vv is a variable of the RR-algebra SS;

  2. (2)(2)

    The R⁡[t]R[t]-algebra S⁡[t]/(v−t)S[t]/(v-t) is isomorphic to a polynomial ring in n−1n-1 variables over R⁡[t]R[t].

Proof.

If vv is a variable, then there exists f∈AutR⁡(S)f\in\Aut_{R}(S) such that f⁡(v)=x1f(v)=x_{1}. Using the natural inclusion AutR⁡(S)↪AutR⁡[t]⁡(S⁡[t])\Aut_{R}(S)\hookrightarrow\Aut_{R[t]}(S[t]), we get isomorphisms of R⁡[t]R[t]-algebras

S⁡[t]/(v−t)⟶≃S⁡[t]/(x1−t)⟶≃R⁡[x2,…,xn,t]⟶≃R⁡[t]​[x2,…,xn].S[t]/(v-t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}S[t]/(x_{1}-t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}R[x_{2},\dots,x_{n},t]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}R[t][x_{2},\dots,x_{n}].

Conversely, suppose that the R⁡[t]R[t]-algebra S⁡[t]/(v−t)S[t]/(v-t) is isomorphic to a polynomial ring in n−1n-1 variables over R⁡[t]R[t]. This yields an R⁡[t]R[t]-isomorphism ψ:S⁡[t]/(t−v)⟶≃R⁡[t]​[x2,…,xn]\psi\colon S[t]/(t-v)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}R[t][x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]. We then compose the isomorphisms of RR-algebras

S=R⁡[x1,…,xn]⟶≃S⁡[t]/(t−v)⟶ψR⁡[t]​[x2,…,xn]f↦f+(t−v)⋅S⁡[t]\begin{array}[]{cccccccc}S=R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&S[t]/(t-v)&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\psi}}{{\longrightarrow}}&R[t][x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]\\ f&\mapsto&f+(t-v)\cdot S[t]&&\end{array}

and

R⁡[t]​[x2,…,xn]⟶≃R⁡[x1,…,xn]f⁡(t,x2,…,xn)↦f⁡(x1,x2,…,xn)\begin{array}[]{ccc}R[t][x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\\ f(t,x_{2},\dots,x_{n})&\mapsto&f(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\end{array}

and obtain an element of AutR⁡(S)\Aut_{R}(S) that sends vv onto x1x_{1}. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Let k be a field, let k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be the polynomial ring in n≥1n\geq 1 variables over k and let w∈k​[x1,…,xn]w\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be a variable of this k-algebra.

Then k​[w]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] is factorially closed in k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], i.e. for all f,g∈k​[x1,…,xn]∖{0}f,g\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\{0\}, we have f​g∈k​[w]⇔f∈k​[w]​ and ​g∈k​[w].fg\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w]\Leftrightarrow f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w]\text{ and }g\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w].

Proof.

If f∈k​[w]f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] and g∈k​[w]g\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w], then f​g∈k​[w]fg\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w], since k​[w]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] is a subring of k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Conversely, suppose that f​g∈k​[w]fg\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w]. Choose ψ∈Autk⁡(k​[x1,…,xn])\psi\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]) such that ψ⁡(w)=x1\psi(w)=x_{1}. Then, ψ⁡(f),ψ⁡(g)∈k​[x1,…,xn]\psi(f),\psi(g)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] are two polynomials such that ψ⁡(f)⋅ψ⁡(g)∈k​[x1]\psi(f)\cdot\psi(g)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1}]. For each i≥2i\geq 2, the degree in xix_{i} satisfies degxi⁡(ψ⁡(f))+degxi⁡(ψ⁡(f))=degxi⁡(ψ⁡(f)⋅ψ⁡(g))=0\deg_{x_{i}}(\psi(f))+\deg_{x_{i}}(\psi(f))=\deg_{x_{i}}(\psi(f)\cdot\psi(g))=0, so degxi⁡(ψ⁡(f))=degxi⁡(ψ⁡(f))=0\deg_{x_{i}}(\psi(f))=\deg_{x_{i}}(\psi(f))=0 since both elements are non-zero. Hence, ψ⁡(f),ψ⁡(g)∈k​[x1]\psi(f),\psi(g)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1}]. Applying ψ−1\psi^{-1}, we get f∈k​[w]f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] and g∈k​[w]g\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w]. ∎

3.1. Variables of polynomial rings in two variables

We will need the following two technical lemmas:

Lemma 3.5.

Let k be a field, let ww be a variable of the k-algebra k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] and let v∈k​[x,y]v\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] be a polynomial. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)(1)

    v∈k​[w]v\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w];

  2. (2)(2)

    For each u∈k​[w]u\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w], the elements uu and vv are algebraically dependent over k.

  3. (3)(3)

    There exists u∈k​[w]∖ku\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w]\setminus\mathbf{\textbf{k}} such that uu and vv are algebraically dependent over k.

Proof.

The implications (1)⇒(2)⇒(3)(\ref{vkw1})\Rightarrow(\ref{vkw2})\Rightarrow(\ref{vkw3}) being clear, we only need to prove (3)⇒(1)(\ref{vkw3})\Rightarrow(\ref{vkw1}). Replacing vv and ww with f⁡(v)f(v) and f⁡(w)f(w), for some f∈Autk⁡(k​[x,y])f\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]), we can assume that w=xw=x. Denoting by k¯\overline{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} the algebraic closure of k, we have k¯​[x]∩k​[x,y]=k​[x]\overline{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}[x]\cap\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x], so we can assume that k=k¯\mathbf{\textbf{k}}=\overline{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

We then consider the morphism τ:𝔸k2→𝔸k2\tau\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by (x,y)↦(u⁡(x),v⁡(x,y))(x,y)\mapsto(u(x),v(x,y)), which is dominant if and only if u,vu,v are algebraically independent over k. It remains then to see that τ\tau is dominant if u∈k​[x]∖ku\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x]\setminus\mathbf{\textbf{k}} and v∉k​[x]v\not\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x]. Let v⁡(x,y)=∑i=0dvi​(x)​yiv(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}v_{i}(x)y^{i}, where vd≠0v_{d}\neq 0 and d>0d>0. For a general a∈ka\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}, u⁡(x)=au(x)=a has a solution x0x_{0} such that vd​(x0)≠0v_{d}(x_{0})\neq 0, since k is algebraically closed. Hence v⁡(x0,y)=bv(x_{0},y)=b has a solution for all b∈kb\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}. This proves that τ\tau is dominant. ∎

Lemma 3.6.

Let k be a field, let p∈k​[t]p\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] be an irreducible element and let kp=k​[t]/(p)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]/(p) be the corresponding residue field. Let u,v∈k​[t]​[x,y]u,v\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t][x,y] be elements such that k​(t)​[u,v]=k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[u,v]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]. Then, the classes u0,v0∈kp​[x,y]u_{0},v_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] of u,vu,v satisfy one of the following properties, depending on the Jacobian determinant ν=∂u∂x⋅∂v∂y−∂u∂y⋅∂v∂x∈k​[t]∖{0}\nu=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]\setminus\{0\}:

  1. (1)(1)

    If pp divides ν\nu, then u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are algebraically dependent over kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}.

  2. (2)(2)

    If pp does not divide ν\nu, then kp​[u0,v0]=kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[u_{0},v_{0}]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y]. In particular, both u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are variables of the kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}-algebra kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y].

Proof.

Since k​(t)​[u,v]=k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[u,v]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], there are polynomials P,Q∈k​(t)​[X,Y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[X,Y] such that P⁡(u,v)=xP(u,v)=x, Q⁡(u,v)=yQ(u,v)=y. Moreover, the polynomial ν=∂u∂x⋅∂v∂y−∂u∂y⋅∂v∂x∈k​[t,x,y]\nu=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] belongs to k​(t)∗\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)^{*} and thus to k​[t]∖{0}\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]\setminus\{0\}. The element ν0=∂u0∂x⋅∂v0∂y−∂u0∂y⋅∂v0∂x\nu_{0}=\frac{\partial u_{0}}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{\partial v_{0}}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial u_{0}}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{\partial v_{0}}{\partial x} is then the class of ν\nu in kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}.

We write P=P~αP=\frac{\tilde{P}}{\alpha}, Q=Q~βQ=\frac{\tilde{Q}}{\beta}, where P~,Q~∈k​[t]​[X,Y]\tilde{P},\tilde{Q}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t][X,Y], α,β∈k​[t]∖{0}\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]\setminus\{0\} and such that pp does not divide both α\alpha and P~\tilde{P} (and the same for β\beta and Q~\tilde{Q}). We then get

P~0​(u0,v0)=α0​x,Q~0​(u0,v0)=β0​y\tilde{P}_{0}(u_{0},v_{0})=\alpha_{0}x\,,\quad\tilde{Q}_{0}(u_{0},v_{0})=\beta_{0}y

where P~0,Q~0∈kp​[X,Y]\tilde{P}_{0},\tilde{Q}_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[X,Y] are the classes of P~,Q~\tilde{P},\tilde{Q} and α0,β0∈kp\alpha_{0},\beta_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} are the classes of α,β\alpha,\beta.

If α0\alpha_{0} and β0\beta_{0} are not equal to zero, then kp​[u0,v0]=kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[u_{0},v_{0}]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y]. In particular, u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are variables of the kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}-algebra kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] and ν0∈kp∗\nu_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}^{*}, so pp does not divide ν\nu.

If α0=0\alpha_{0}=0, then P~0≠0\tilde{P}_{0}\not=0 and P~0​(u0,v0)=0\tilde{P}_{0}(u_{0},v_{0})=0 implies that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are algebraically dependent over kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}. The same conclusion holds when β0=0\beta_{0}=0. In both cases, the Jacobian determinant ν0\nu_{0} is equal to zero, so pp divides ν\nu.

This yields (1) and (2). ∎

We recall the following classical result, essentially equivalent to the Jung-van der Kulk theorem:

Lemma 3.7.

Let k be a field, let k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] be the polynomial ring in two variables over k, let f∈Autk⁡(k​[x,y])f\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]) and u=f⁡(x),v=f⁡(y)∈k​[x,y]u=f(x),v=f(y)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. If deg⁡(u)≥deg⁡(v)>1\deg(u)\geq\deg(v)>1, then there exists a polynomial PP with coefficients in k such that deg⁡(u−P⁡(v))<deg⁡(u)\deg(u-P(v))<\deg(u).

Proof.

By van der Kulk’s Theorem all automorphisms of k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] are tame [Jun42, vdK53]. The statement is then a direct consequence of [vdE00, Corollary 5.1.6]. ∎

The following result is needed in the sequel. When the characteristic of k is zero, and p=tp=t, it follows from [Fur02, Theorem 4]. We adapt here the proof of [Fur02] for our purpose.

Lemma 3.8.

Let k be a field, let p∈k​[t]p\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] be an irreducible element and let kp=k​[t]/(p)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]/(p) be the corresponding residue field. If v∈k​[t,x,y]v\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], then its class in kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] is an element which belongs to kp​[w]⊂kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[w]\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] for some variable ww of the kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}-algebra kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y].

Proof.

Let f∈Autk​(t)⁡(k​(t)​[x,y])f\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]) such that f⁡(x)=vf(x)=v, and let us define u=f⁡(y)u=f(y). We denote by v0∈kp​[x,y]v_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] the class of vv and will use the degree of polynomials in x,yx,y with coefficients in k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t) or kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}.

If deg⁡(v)=1\deg(v)=1, then deg⁡(v0)≤1\deg(v_{0})\leq 1. If v0∈kpv_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} the result follows by taking any variable for ww, for instance w=xw=x. Otherwise, v0=α​x+β​y+γv_{0}=\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma for some α,β,γ∈kp\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} with (α,β)≠(0,0)(\alpha,\beta)\not=(0,0). This implies that w=α​x+β​yw=\alpha x+\beta y is a variable, as it is the component of an element of GL2⁡(kp)\GL_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}), and the result follows.

We can thus assume that deg⁡(v)>1\deg(v)>1 and prove the result by induction on the pair (deg⁡(v),deg⁡(u))(\deg(v),\deg(u)), ordered lexicographically.

(i)(i) If deg⁡(u)≥deg⁡(v)\deg(u)\geq\deg(v), then there exists a polynomial P∈k​(t)​[X]P\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[X] such that deg⁡(u−P⁡(v))<deg⁡(u)\deg(u-P(v))<\deg(u) (Lemma 3.7). We can thus apply induction hypothesis to (u−P⁡(v),v)(u-P(v),v), since k​(t)​[u,v]=k​(t)​[u−P⁡(v),v]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[u,v]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[u-P(v),v], and obtain the result.

(i​i)(ii) If deg⁡(u)<deg⁡(v)\deg(u)<\deg(v), we first replace uu with u−λu-\lambda for some λ∈k​(t)\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t) and assume that u∈k​(t)​[x,y]u\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y] is a polynomial in x,yx,y with no constant term. We then replace uu with q​uqu for some q∈k​(t)∗q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)^{*} and assume that u∈k​[t]​[x,y]u\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t][x,y] and the greatest common divisor in k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] of the coefficients of uu (as a polynomial in x,yx,y) is equal to 11. One can then define the class u0∈kp​[x,y]u_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] of uu, which is not equal to zero. Moreover, u0u_{0} does not belong to kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}, since u0u_{0} has no constant term.

If v0v_{0} is a variable of the kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}-algebra kp​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y], then we are done. Otherwise, u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are algebraically dependent over kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} (Lemma 3.6).

Since the pair (deg⁡(v),deg⁡(u))(\deg(v),\deg(u)) is smaller than (deg⁡(u),deg⁡(v))(\deg(u),\deg(v)), we can apply induction hypothesis and get a variable w∈kp​[x,y]w\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[x,y] such that u0∈kp​[w]u_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[w]. The fact that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are algebraically dependent over kp\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} and that u0∉kpu_{0}\not\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p} imply that v0∈kp​[w]v_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}_{p}[w] (Lemma 3.5). ∎

We finish this section with several results relating variables and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundles.

Lemma 3.9.

Let k be a field and let P∈k​[x,y]P\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)(1)

    The polynomial PP is a variable of the k-algebra k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y].

  2. (2)(2)

    The k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]-algebra k​[t,x,y]/(P−t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]/(P-t) is a polynomial ring in one variable over k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t].

  3. (3)(3)

    The k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]/(P−t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]/(P-t) is a polynomial ring in one variable over k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t).

  4. (4)(4)

    The morphism 𝔸k2→𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by (x,y)↦P⁡(x,y)(x,y)\mapsto P(x,y) is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle.

  5. (5)(5)

    The morphism 𝔸k2→𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by (x,y)↦P⁡(x,y)(x,y)\mapsto P(x,y) is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle over some dense open subset U⊂𝔸k1U\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

Proof.

(1)⇔(2)(\ref{Pvkxy})\Leftrightarrow(\ref{Pktxy}) follows from Lemma 3.3.

(1)⇔(4)(\ref{Pvkxy})\Leftrightarrow(\ref{Ptrivial}): By definition, (1)(\ref{Pvkxy}) is equivalent to the existence of f∈Autk⁡(k​[x,y])f\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]) such that f⁡(x)=Pf(x)=P. As f=φ∗f=\varphi^{*} for some φ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k2)\varphi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}), this is equivalent to ask for φ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k2)\varphi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) that prx∘φ\pr_{x}\circ\varphi is the map (x,y)↦P⁡(x,y)(x,y)\mapsto P(x,y), where prx:𝔸k2→𝔸k1\pr_{x}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is given by (x,y)↦x(x,y)\mapsto x. This yields the equivalence (1)⇔(4)(\ref{Pvkxy})\Leftrightarrow(\ref{Ptrivial}).

(2)⇒(3)(\ref{Pktxy})\Rightarrow(\ref{Pktxyfield}) is trivially true.

(3)⇒(5)(\ref{Pktxyfield})\Rightarrow(\ref{Ploctrivial}): Assertion (3)(\ref{Pktxyfield}) corresponds to say that the generic fibre of (x,y)↦P⁡(x,y)(x,y)\mapsto P(x,y) is isomorphic to 𝔸k​(t)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}. This yields (5)(\ref{Ploctrivial}).

(5)⇒(1):(\ref{Ploctrivial})\Rightarrow(\ref{Pvkxy}): Assume that the subset UU given in (5)(\ref{Ploctrivial}) contains a k-rational point. Replacing PP with P+λP+\lambda, λ∈k\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}, one can assume that 00 belongs to the open subset UU. One then observes that the curve Γ⊂𝔸k2\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by P=0P=0 is isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} and equivalent to a line by a birational map of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, hence can be contracted by a birational map of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}. By [BFH16, Proposition 2.29], there exists an automorphism φ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k2)\varphi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) which sends Γ\Gamma onto the line given by x=0x=0. This implies that PP is a variable of the k-algebra k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y].

If UU contains no k-rational point, then k is a finite field and thus it is perfect. For a finite Galois extension k′⊃k\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}\supset\mathbf{\textbf{k}} the subset UU contains a k′\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}-rational point. By the argument above, PP is a variable of the k′\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}-algebra k′​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[x,y] and hence k′​[x,y]=k′​[P,Q]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[x,y]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[P,Q] for some Q∈k′​[x,y]Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[x,y]. Since PP is a polynomial with coefficients in k, it is fixed under the action of the Galois group G=Gal⁡(k′/k)G=\Gal(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}/\mathbf{\textbf{k}}) on k​[x,y]=k′​[P,Q]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[P,Q]. For each σ∈G\sigma\in G, there exists (aσ,bσ)∈(k′)∗⋉k′​[T](a_{\sigma},b_{\sigma})\in(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime})^{\ast}\ltimes\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[T] with

σ⁡(Q)=aσ​Q+bσ​(P).\sigma(Q)=a_{\sigma}Q+b_{\sigma}(P).

We can then find d≥0d\geq 0 such that {bσ∣σ∈G}\{b_{\sigma}\mid\sigma\in G\} is contained in the finite dimensional k′\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}-vector subspace Vd={f∈k′​[T]∣deg⁡(P)≤d}⊂k′​[T]V_{d}=\{f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[T]\mid\deg(P)\leq d\}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime}[T]. Thus σ↦(aσ,bσ)\sigma\mapsto(a_{\sigma},b_{\sigma}) defines an element of H1​(G,(k′)∗⋉Vd)H^{1}(G,(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime})^{\ast}\ltimes V_{d}). As H1​(G,(k′)∗)={1}H^{1}(G,(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime})^{\ast})=\{1\} and H1​(G,Vd)={1}H^{1}(G,V_{d})=\{1\} [Ser68, Proposition 1, 2, Chp. X], we have H1​(G,(k′)∗⋉Vd)={1}H^{1}(G,(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\prime})^{\ast}\ltimes V_{d})=\{1\}. The fact that (aσ,bσ)(a_{\sigma},b_{\sigma}) is a trivial cocycle corresponds to the existence of a polynomial Q0∈k​[x,y]Q_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] such that k​[P,Q0]=k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[P,Q_{0}]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. This implies that PP is a variable of the k-algebra k​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. ∎

We recall the following classical result:

Lemma 3.10.

Let k be a field, let ZZ be an affine variety over k, all of its irreducible components being surfaces, let U⊆𝔸k1U\subseteq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} be a dense open subset and let π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U be a dominant morphism. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)(1)

    The morphism π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle.

  2. (2)(2)

    The morphism π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U is a locally trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle.

  3. (3)(3)

    For each maximal ideal 𝔪⊂k​[U]\mathfrak{m}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U], the fibre π−1​(𝔪)⊂Z\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\subset Z is isomorphic to 𝔸κ⁡(𝔪)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\kappa(\mathfrak{m})} and the generic fibre of π\pi is isomorphic to 𝔸k​(t)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}.

Proof.

The implications (1)⇒(2)⇒(3)\eqref{PPPtrivialA1bundle}\Rightarrow\eqref{PPPloctrivialA1bundle}\Rightarrow\eqref{PPPeachfibA1} are obvious. Assume (3) holds. Since each irreducible component of ZZ has dimension two, it follows that each of these irreducible components is mapped dominantly onto UU via π\pi. Thus π\pi is flat. By [Asa87, Corollary 3.2] it follows now from (3) that k​[Z]𝔪\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[Z]_{\mathfrak{m}} is a polynomial ring in one variable over k​[U]𝔪\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U]_{\mathfrak{m}} for all maximal ideals 𝔪⊂k​[U]\mathfrak{m}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U]. Hence, by [BCW77], the morphism π\pi is a vector bundle with respect to the Zariski topology and since k​[U]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U] is a principal ideal domain, π\pi is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle. ∎

Lemma 3.11.

Let k be a field, P∈k​[t,x,y]P\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] be a polynomial which is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], let U⊂𝔸k1=Spec⁡(k​[t])U\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]) be a dense open subset, let Z⊂U×𝔸k2=Spec⁡(k​[U]​[x,y])Z\subset U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U][x,y]) be the hypersurface given by P=0P=0 and let π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U be the morphism (t,x,y)↦t(t,x,y)\mapsto t. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)(i)

    PP is a variable of the k​[U]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U]-algebra k​[U]​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U][x,y];

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    There is an isomorphism φ:U×𝔸k1⟶≃Z\varphi\colon U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}Z such that π​φ\pi\varphi is the projection (t,x)↦t(t,x)\mapsto t;

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    The morphism π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle;

  4. (i​v)(iv)

    The morphism π:Z→U\pi\colon Z\to U is a locally trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle;

  5. (v)(v)

    For each maximal ideal 𝔪⊂k​[U]\mathfrak{m}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U], the fibre π−1​(𝔪)⊂Z\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\subset Z is isomorphic to 𝔸κ⁡(𝔪)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\kappa(\mathfrak{m})}.

Proof.

(i)⇒(ii)(\ref{PPVarktU})\Rightarrow(\ref{PPisoA2fibrU}): If PP is a variable of the k​[U]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U]-algebra k​[U]​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U][x,y], there exists f∈Autk​[U]⁡(k​[U]​[x,y])f\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U]}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[U][x,y]) such that f⁡(x)=Pf(x)=P. The element ff is then equal to ψ∗\psi^{*} for some ψ∈Aut⁡(U×𝔸k2)\psi\in\Aut(U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) such that π​ψ=π\pi\psi=\pi. Hence, ψ⁡(Z)\psi(Z) is the closed subset of U×𝔸k2U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by x=0x=0. Let θ:U×𝔸k2→U×𝔸k1\theta\colon U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} be the projection given by (t,x,y)↦(t,y)(t,x,y)\mapsto(t,y). The composition θ∘ψ\theta\circ\psi restricts to an isomorphism Z⟶≃U×𝔸k1Z\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} that we denote by φ−1\varphi^{-1}. Thus pr1∘φ−1=π\mathrm{pr}_{1}\circ\varphi^{-1}=\pi, where pr1:U×𝔸k1→U\mathrm{pr}_{1}\colon U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to U is the projection on the first factor. This yields (ii)(\ref{PPisoA2fibrU}).

(ii)⇔(iii)(\ref{PPisoA2fibrU})\Leftrightarrow(\ref{PPtrivialA1bundleU}): is the definition of a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle.

(iii)⇒(iv)⇒(v)(\ref{PPtrivialA1bundleU})\Rightarrow(\ref{PPloctrivialA1bundleU})\Rightarrow(\ref{PPeachfibA1U}) are obvious.

(v)⇒(i)(\ref{PPeachfibA1U})\Rightarrow(\ref{PPVarktU}): This follows from the implication (3)⇒(1)\eqref{PPPeachfibA1}\Rightarrow\eqref{PPPtrivialA1bundle} of Lemma 3.10.

∎

Corollary 3.12.

Let k be a field, let P∈k​[t,x,y]P\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] be a polynomial which is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], let Z⊂𝔸k3=Spec⁡(k​[t,x,y])Z\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) be the hypersurface given by P=0P=0 and let π:Z→𝔸k1\pi\colon Z\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} be the morphism (t,x,y)↦t(t,x,y)\mapsto t. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)(i)

    PP is a variable of the k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]-algebra k​[t]​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t][x,y];

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    There is an isomorphism φ:𝔸k2⟶≃Z\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}Z such that π​φ\pi\varphi is the projection (t,x)↦t(t,x)\mapsto t;

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    There is an isomorphism φ:𝔸k2⟶≃Z\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}Z;

  4. (i​v)(iv)

    The morphism π:Z→𝔸k1\pi\colon Z\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle;

  5. (v)(v)

    The morphism π:Z→𝔸k1\pi\colon Z\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is a locally trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle;

  6. (v​i)(vi)

    For each maximal ideal 𝔪⊂k​[t]\mathfrak{m}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], the fibre π−1​(𝔪)⊂Z\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\subset Z is isomorphic to 𝔸κ⁡(𝔪)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\kappa(\mathfrak{m})}.

Proof.

Applying Lemma 3.11 with U=𝔸k1U={\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, we obtain the equivalence between (i)(\ref{PPVarkt})-(ii)(\ref{PPisoA2fibr})-(iv)(\ref{PPtrivialA1bundle})-(v)(\ref{PPloctrivialA1bundle})-(vi)(\ref{PPeachfibA1}).

We then observe that (ii)(\ref{PPisoA2fibr}) implies (iii)(\ref{PPisoA2}). It remains then to prove (iii)⇒(iv)(\ref{PPisoA2})\Rightarrow(\ref{PPtrivialA1bundle}). As PP is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], the generic fibre of π:Z→𝔸k1\pi\colon Z\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is isomorphic to 𝔸k​(t)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}, so π\pi is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle over some dense open subset U⊂𝔸k1U\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}. The fact that ZZ is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} implies then that π\pi is a trivial 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}-bundle. (Implication (5)⇒(4)(\ref{Ploctrivial})\Rightarrow(\ref{Ptrivial}) of Lemma 3.9). ∎

3.2. Non-trivial embeddings in positive characteristic

In this paragraph, we recall the existence of non-trivial embeddings in positive characteristic. The family of examples that we give below seems classical (the case 𝔸k1↪𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} with parameters equal to 11 corresponds in particular to [vdE00, Exercise 5(iii) in §​5\lx@sectionsign 5]). We give the (simple) proof here for a lack of a precise reference and for self-containedness.

Lemma 3.13.

For each field k of characteristic p>0p>0, each a∈ka\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}, b∈k∗b\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast} and each integer q≥0q\geq 0, the morphism

ρ:𝔸k1↪𝔸k2u↦(up2,1b​(a​up​q+u))\begin{array}[]{rrcl}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\\ &u&\mapsto&(u^{p^{2}},\frac{1}{b}(au^{pq}+u))\end{array}

is a closed embedding, with image being the closed curve of 𝔸k2=Spec⁡(k​[x,y]){\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]) given by

x+ap2​xp​q−bp2​yp2=0.x+a^{p^{2}}x^{pq}-b^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}=0.
Proof.

We first compute the equality

bp​(1b​(a​up​q+u))p−ap​(up2)q=(ap​up2​q+up)−ap​up2​q=up,b^{p}\left(\frac{1}{b}(au^{pq}+u)\right)^{p}-a^{p}(u^{p^{2}})^{q}=(a^{p}u^{p^{2}q}+u^{p})-a^{p}u^{p^{2}q}=u^{p},

which shows that ρ⁡(𝔸k1)\rho({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) is contained in the closed curve Γ⊂𝔸k2\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by P=0P=0, where P=x−(bp​yp−ap​xq)p=x−bp2​yp2+ap2​xq​p∈k​[x,y]P=x-(b^{p}y^{p}-a^{p}x^{q})^{p}=x-b^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}+a^{p^{2}}x^{qp}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. The equality also yields up∈k​[up2,1b​(a​up​q+u)]u^{p}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[u^{p^{2}},\frac{1}{b}(au^{pq}+u)] and thus yields k​[up2,1b​(a​up​q+u)]=k​[u]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[u^{p^{2}},\frac{1}{b}(au^{pq}+u)]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[u], which implies that ρ\rho is a closed embedding. It remains to see that the degree of ρ\rho (maximum of the degree of both components) is equal to the degree of PP, to obtain that PP is irreducible and that it defines the irreducible curve ρ⁡(𝔸k1)\rho({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}). For a=0a=0, this follows, since deg⁡(ρ)=p2=deg⁡(P)\deg(\rho)=p^{2}=\deg(P). For a≠0a\not=0, we have deg⁡(ρ)=max⁡(p2,p​q)=deg⁡(P)\deg(\rho)=\max(p^{2},pq)=\deg(P). ∎

To show that the above embeddings are not equivalent to the standard one, when q≥2q\geq 2 is not a multiple of pp and a,b≠0a,b\not=0, one could make argument on the degree of the components (no one divides the other) or can use the characterisation of variables given in Lemma 3.3 to show that P=x+ap2​xp​q−bp2​yp2∈k​[x,y]P=x+a^{p^{2}}x^{pq}-b^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] is not a variable, by proving that k​[x,y,t]/(P−t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y,t]/(P-t) is not a polynomial ring in one variable over k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], as we do in Lemma 3.14 below. The second way has the advantage to give examples in any dimension (see Proposition 3.16). This is related to the forms of the affine line over non-perfect fields (for more details on this subject, see [Rus70]).

Lemma 3.14.

For each field k of characteristic p>0p>0, each b∈k∗b\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast} and each integer q≥2q\geq 2, not a multiple of pp, the curve

Γ=Spec⁡(k​(t)​[x,y]/(x+ap2​xp​q−bp2​yp2−t))\Gamma=\Spec\left(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]/(x+a^{p^{2}}x^{pq}-b^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}-t)\right)

is not isomorphic to 𝔸k​(t)1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}, but after extension of scalars to k​(t1/p)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p}) we have an isomorphism

Γk​(t1/p)⟶≃𝔸k​(t1/p)1.\Gamma_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p})}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p})}.
Proof.

After extending the scalars to k​(t1/p2)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}}), the curve Γ\Gamma becomes

Γk​(t1/p2)=Spec⁡(k​(t1/p2)​[x,y]/(x+ap2​xp​q−bp2​yp2−t))=Spec⁡(k​(t1/p2)​[x,y]/(x+ap2​xp​q−bp2​(y+t1/p2b)p2)).\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Gamma_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}})}&=&\Spec\left(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}})[x,y]/(x+a^{p^{2}}x^{pq}-b^{p^{2}}y^{p^{2}}-t)\right)\\ &=&\Spec\left(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}})[x,y]/\left(x+a^{p^{2}}x^{pq}-b^{p^{2}}\left(y+\frac{t^{1/p^{2}}}{b}\right)^{p^{2}}\right)\right)\,.\end{array}

Replacing yy with y+t1/p2by+\frac{t^{1/p^{2}}}{b} and applying Lemma 3.13 we obtain an isomorphism

𝔸k​(t1/p2)1⟶≃Γk​(t1/p2)u↦(up2,1b​(a​up​q+u−t1/p2)).\begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}})}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\Gamma_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p^{2}})}\\ u&\mapsto&\left(u^{p^{2}},\frac{1}{b}\left(au^{pq}+u-t^{1/p^{2}}\right)\right)\,.\end{array}

Replacing then uu with u+t1/p2u+t^{1/p^{2}} we get an isomorphism defined over k​(t1/p)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p}):

ν:𝔸k​(t1/p)1⟶≃Γk​(t1/p)u↦(up2+t,1b​(a​(up+t1/p)q+u)).\begin{array}[]{rrcl}\nu\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p})}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\Gamma_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p})}\\ &u&\mapsto&\left(u^{p^{2}}+t,\frac{1}{b}\left(a\left(u^{p}+t^{1/p}\right)^{q}+u\right)\right)\,.\end{array}

It remains that no isomorphism ν^:𝔸k​(t)1⟶≃Γk​(t)\hat{\nu}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Gamma_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)} exists. If ν^\hat{\nu} exists, then ν−1​ν^∈Aut⁡(𝔸k​(t1/p)1)\nu^{-1}\hat{\nu}\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p})}) would be given by u↦α​u+βu\mapsto\alpha u+\beta, with α,β∈k​(t1/p)\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t^{1/p}), α≠0\alpha\not=0. The second coordinate of ν^​(u)\hat{\nu}(u) would then be

1b​(a​((α​u+β)p+t1/p)q+(α​u+β))∈k​(t)​[u].\frac{1}{b}\left(a\left((\alpha u+\beta)^{p}+t^{1/p}\right)^{q}+(\alpha u+\beta)\right)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[u]\,.

The coefficient of uu being αb\frac{\alpha}{b}, we get α∈k​(t)\alpha\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t). Remembering that q≥2q\geq 2, the coefficient of up⁡(q−1)u^{p(q-1)} is equal to ab​q​αp⁡(q−1)​(βp+t1/p)\frac{a}{b}q\alpha^{p(q-1)}(\beta^{p}+t^{1/p}). As βp∈k​(t)\beta^{p}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t) we have βp+t1/p∉k​(t)\beta^{p}+t^{1/p}\notin\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t). Impossible, since qq is not a multiple of pp and α≠0\alpha\not=0. ∎

Corollary 3.15.

For each field k of characteristic p>0p>0, each integer q≥2q\geq 2 which is not a multiple of pp, each λ,μ∈k∗\lambda,\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and each integer n≥2n\geq 2, the polynomial

f=x1+λ​x1p​q+μ​x2p2∈k​[x1,x2]⊂k​[x1,…,xn]f=x_{1}+\lambda x_{1}^{pq}+\mu x_{2}^{p^{2}}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},x_{2}]\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]

is not a variable of the k-algebra k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Proof.

Showing that ff is not a variable of k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is equivalent to ask that the k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]-algebra k​[x1,x2,…,xn,t]/(f−t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n},t]/(f-t) is not a polynomial ring in n−1n-1 variables over k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] (Lemma 3.3). It suffices then to show that An=k​(t)​[x1,…,xn]/(f−t)A_{n}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/(f-t) is not a polynomial ring in n−1n-1 variables over k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t).

We first prove the result for n=2n=2. By extending the scalars, we can assume that λ=ap2\lambda=a^{p^{2}} and μ=−bp2\mu=-b^{p^{2}} for some a,b∈k∗a,b\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. Lemma 3.14 then shows that A2=k​(t)​[x1,x2]/(f−t)A_{2}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x_{1},x_{2}]/(f-t) is not a polynomial ring in one variable.

As An=A2​[x3,…,xn]A_{n}=A_{2}[x_{3},\dots,x_{n}], the positive answer to the cancellation problem for curves [AHE72] implies that AnA_{n} is not a polynomial ring in n−1n-1 variables over k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t) for each n≥2n\geq 2. ∎

Proposition 3.16.

For each field k of characteristic p>0p>0, each integer q≥2q\geq 2 which is not a multiple of pp, each a∈k∗a\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and each n≥1n\geq 1, the morphism

ρ:𝔸n↪𝔸n+1(x1,…,xn)↦(x1p2,a​x1p​q+x1,x2,…,xn)\begin{array}[]{rrcl}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{n}&\hookrightarrow&{\mathbb{A}}^{n+1}\\ &(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})&\mapsto&(x_{1}^{p^{2}},ax_{1}^{pq}+x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\end{array}

is a closed embedding, which is not equivalent to the standard one.

Proof.

It follows from Lemma 3.13 that ρ\rho is a closed embedding and that its image is given by the hypersurface with equation f=0f=0, where

f=x1+ap2​x1p​q−x2p2∈k​[x1,x2]⊂k​[x1,…,xn].f=x_{1}+a^{p^{2}}x_{1}^{pq}-x_{2}^{p^{2}}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},x_{2}]\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

It remains to show that ff is not a variable of k​[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], which follows from Corollary 3.15. ∎

By Lemma 3.8, g⁡(0,x,y)g(0,x,y) belongs to k​[w]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] for some variable w∈k​[x,y]w\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. The fact that g⁡(0,x,y)∈h0⋅k​[x,y]∖{0}g(0,x,y)\in h_{0}\cdot\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]\setminus\{0\} implies then that h0∈k​[w]h_{0}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] (Lemma 3.4), contradicting the hypothesis. ∎

Corollary 4.2.

Let k be a field and

R=k​[t,u,x,y]/(tn​u−h⁡(t,x,y))R=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(t^{n}u-h(t,x,y))

where n≥1n\geq 1 and h∈k​[t,x,y]h\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] is a polynomial such that h0=h⁡(0,x,y)∈k​[x,y]h_{0}=h(0,x,y)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y] does not belong to k​[w]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[w] for each variable w∈k​[x,y].w\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x,y]. Writing II the ideal (tn,h)⊂k​[t,x,y](t^{n},h)\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y], we obtain a group isomorphism

Autk​[t]⁡(R)⟶≃{ψ∈Autk​[t]⁡(k​[t,x,y])∣ψ⁡(I)=I}φ↦φ|k​[t,x,y]\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]}(R)&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\{\psi\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y])\mid\psi(I)=I\}\\ \varphi&\mapsto&\varphi|_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]}\end{array}
Proof.

According to Lemma 4.1(4), every element φ∈Autk​[t]⁡(R)\varphi\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]}(R) preserves k​[t,x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] and II, and thus restricts to an element ψ∈Autk​[t]⁡(k​[t,x,y])\psi\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) that preserves II.

Conversely, each automorphism ψ∈Autk​[t]⁡(k​[t,x,y])\psi\in\Aut_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) that preserves II induces an automorphism of R=k​[t,x,y]​[Itn]=k​[t,x,y]​[htn]R=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y][\frac{I}{t^{n}}]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y][\frac{h}{t^{n}}]. This latter is uniquely determined by ψ\psi, since the morphism Spec⁡(R)→Spec⁡(k​[t,x,y])\Spec(R)\to\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) given by the inclusion k​[t,x,y]↪R\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]\hookrightarrow R is birational. ∎

Remark 4.3.

According to [KZ99, Definition 1.1 and Proposition 1.1], Spec⁡(R)\Spec(R) is the affine modification of 𝔸k3=Spec⁡(k​[t,x,y]){\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) with locus (I,tn)(I,t^{n}). It is thus natural that every automorphism of 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} fixing the ideal lift to an automorphism of Spec⁡(R)\Spec(R). The interesting part of Corollary 4.2 consists then in saying that all automorphisms of the k​[t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t]-algebra RR are of this form.

4.2. Application of liftings to the case of SL2\SL_{2}

We will apply Corollary 4.2 to the variety SL2⊂𝔸4\SL_{2}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{4} given by

SL2={(xtuy)∈𝔸4|xy−tu=1},\SL_{2}=\left\{\left.\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\in{\mathbb{A}}^{4}\right|xy-tu=1\right\},

and obtain Proposition 4.5 below. Before we give a proof, let us recall the following basic facts on the coordinate ring of the variety SL2\SL_{2}.

Lemma 4.4.

Let RR be the coordinate ring of SL2\SL_{2}, i.e. R=k​[t,u,x,y]/(x​y−t​u−1)R=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(xy-tu-1). Then RR is a unique factorisation domain and the units of RR satisfy R∗=k∗R^{\ast}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast}.

Proof.

Since the localisation Rt=k​[t,1t]​[x,y]R_{t}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,\frac{1}{t}][x,y] is a unique factorisation domain, we only have to see that t​RtR is a prime ideal of RR, by [Mat89, Theorem 20.2]. This is the case, since R/t​R≃k​[u,x,y]/(x​y−1)R/tR\simeq\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[u,x,y]/(xy-1) is an integral domain. Moreover, we have R∗⊆(Rt)∗={μtn∣μ∈k∗,n∈ℤ}R^{\ast}\subseteq(R_{t})^{\ast}=\{\mu t^{n}\mid\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*},n\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Since tnt^{n} is invertible in RR if and only if n=0n=0, it follows that R∗=k∗R^{\ast}=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast}. ∎

Corollary 4.6.

The closed embedding

5. Fibered embeddings of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} into SL2\SL_{2} and the proof of Theorem 3

In this section, we study fibred embeddings (as in 1.2).

We will need the following simple description of the morphism η:SL2→𝔸k3\eta\colon\SL_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} already studied in Proposition 4.5:

Lemma 5.1.

Let Γ⊂𝔸k3=Spec⁡(k​[t,x,y])\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]) be the curve given by t=x​y−1=0t=xy-1=0 and let η:B​ℓΓ⁡(𝔸k3)→𝔸k3\eta\colon\Bl_{\Gamma}({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})\to{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} the blow-up of Γ\Gamma. The blow-up of Γ\Gamma can be seen as

The open subset of B​ℓΓ⁡(𝔸k3)\Bl_{\Gamma}({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) given by v≠0v\not=0 is then naturally isomorphic to SL2\SL_{2}, by identifying ((t,x,y),[u:1])((t,x,y),[u:1]) with (t,u,x,y)∈SL2(t,u,x,y)\in\SL_{2}, and the birational morphism η:SL2→𝔸k3\eta\colon\SL_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} sends ((t,x,y),[u:1])((t,x,y),[u:1]) onto (t,x,y)(t,x,y). ∎

In this section, we consider embeddings satisfying the conditions of Proposition 5.4 (or equivalently of Theorem 3(1)) and determine when two of these are equivalent, by proving Theorem 3(2). Remark 5.7.

Lemma 5.6 shows in particular that if HP,HQ⊂SL2H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2} are two hypersurfaces given by two polynomials P,Q∈k​[t,x,y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] as in Theorem 3 (or as in the previous results), and if one of the two integers m,m′∈ℕm,m^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{N}} associated to P,QP,Q is equal to zero, then HP,HQH_{P},H_{Q} are equivalent if and only if m=m′=0m=m^{\prime}=0.

Proposition 5.8.

Let k be any field, let P,Q∈k​[t,x,y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] be polynomials that are variables of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y], and let HP,HQ⊂SL2=Spec⁡(k​[t,u,x,y]/(x​y−t​u−1))H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(xy-tu-1)) and ZP,ZQ⊂𝔸k3=Spec⁡(k​[t,u,x])Z_{P},Z_{Q}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x]) be the hypersurfaces given by P=0P=0 and Q=0Q=0 respectively.

Suppose that HPH_{P} is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} but that ZPZ_{P} is not isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, and that there exists φ∈Aut⁡(SL2)\varphi\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) that sends HPH_{P} onto HQH_{Q}. Then, the following hold:

  1. (1)(1)

    There exists μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} such that φ∗​(t)=μ​t\varphi^{*}(t)=\mu t.

  2. (2)(2)

    The birational map ψ=η​φ​η−1\psi=\eta\varphi\eta^{-1} is an automorphism of 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} which sends ZPZ_{P} onto ZQZ_{Q}, where η:SL2→𝔸k3\eta\colon\SL_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is as before given by (t,u,x,y)↦(t,x,y)(t,u,x,y)\mapsto(t,x,y).

  3. (3)(3)

    There exists m≥1m\geq 1 such that P⁡(0,x,y)P(0,x,y) and Q⁡(0,x,y)Q(0,x,y) are of the form μ​xm​(x−λ)\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda) or μ​ym​(y−λ)\mu y^{m}(y-\lambda) for some μ,λ∈k∗\mu,\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} ((the integer mm is the same for P,QP,Q but μ,λ\mu,\lambda and the choice between xx and yy depend on OPENP,Q)P,Q).

Proof.

Since HPH_{P} is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, the same holds for HQH_{Q}. The hypersurfaces HP,HQ⊂SL2H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2} are thus image of fibred embeddings 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} and there are thus integers m,m′≥0m,m^{\prime}\geq 0 and λ,λ′,μ′,μ∈k∗\lambda,\lambda^{\prime},\mu^{\prime},\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} such that P⁡(0,x,y)∈{μ​xm​(x−λ),μ​ym​(y−λ)}P(0,x,y)\in\{\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda),\mu y^{m}(y-\lambda)\} and Q⁡(0,x,y)∈{μ′​xm′​(x−λ′),μ′​ym′​(y−λ′)}Q(0,x,y)\in\{\mu^{\prime}x^{m^{\prime}}(x-\lambda^{\prime}),\mu^{\prime}y^{m^{\prime}}(y-\lambda^{\prime})\} (Proposition 5.4). Moreover, the fact that ZPZ_{P} is not isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is equivalent to m>0m>0 and to the fact that HPH_{P} is not equivalent to the image ρ1​(𝔸2)\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}) of the standard embedding (Lemma 5.6). As HPH_{P} and HQH_{Q} are equivalent, the same hold for HQH_{Q}, so m′>0m^{\prime}>0.

The main part of the proof consists in proving (1). To do this, one can extend the scalars and assume k to be algebraically closed. We moreover have φ∗​(Q)=ξ​P\varphi^{*}(Q)=\xi P for some ξ∈k∗\xi\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} (follows from Lemma 4.4). Replacing PP with ξ​P\xi P, we can assume that φ∗​(Q)=P\varphi^{*}(Q)=P. For each a∈k∗a\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}, the element φ\varphi then sends HP−aH_{P-a} onto HQ−aH_{Q-a}, where HP−a,HQ−a⊂SL2H_{P-a},H_{Q-a}\subset\SL_{2} are given by the polynomials P−a,Q−a∈k​[t,x,y]P-a,Q-a\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]. If aa is chosen general, then HP−a,HQ−aH_{P-a},H_{Q-a} are smooth hypersurfaces of SL2\SL_{2} (since this is true for a=0a=0), and the same holds for the hypersurfaces ZP−a,ZQ−a⊂𝔸k3Z_{P-a},Z_{Q-a}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by P−aP-a and Q−aQ-a respectively. Since P,QP,Q are variables of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y] and because the tt-projections ZP→𝔸1Z_{P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and ZQ→𝔸1Z_{Q}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} are trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundles over 𝔸k1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} (Lemma 5.2(1)), the polynomials P,QP,Q are also variables of the k​[t,1t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,\frac{1}{t}]-algebra k​[t,1t]​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,\frac{1}{t}][x,y] (follows from Lemma 3.11 with U=𝔸1∖{0}U={\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}). Hence, the same holds for P−aP-a and Q−aQ-a. The morphisms HP−a,HQ−a,ZP−a,ZQ−a→𝔸k1H_{P-a},H_{Q-a},Z_{P-a},Z_{Q-a}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by the projection on tt are therefore trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundles over 𝔸k1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\{0\}. We can thus see these varieties as open subsets of smooth projective surfaces HP−a¯,HQ−a¯,ZP−a¯,ZQ−a¯\overline{H_{P-a}},\overline{H_{Q-a}},\overline{Z_{P-a}},\overline{Z_{Q-a}} obtained by blowing-up some Hirzebruch surfaces, so that the projection on tt is the restriction of the morphism to ℙk1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by a ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-bundle of the Hirzebruch surface and having only one singular fibre. We can moreover assume that the boundary is a union of smooth rational curves of self-intersection 00 or ≤−2\leq-2 (in particular the projectivisation is minimal). Indeed, if a component of the singular fibre has self-intersection −1-1 and is in the boundary, we can contract it, and if the section has self-intersection −1-1, then we blow-up a general point of the smooth fibre contained in the boundary and then contract the strict transform of this fibre to obtain a section of self-intersection 00. The zero fibre of ZP−a→𝔸k1Z_{P-a}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is given by t=μ​xm​(x−λ)−a=0t=\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda)-a=0 or t=μ​ym​(y−λ)−a=0t=\mu y^{m}(y-\lambda)-a=0 and is thus a disjoint union C≃∐i=1m+1𝔸k1C\simeq\coprod_{i=1}^{m+1}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} of m+1m+1 affine curves isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}. Similarly the zero fibre of ZQ−a→𝔸k1Z_{Q-a}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is a disjoint union C′≃∐i=1m′+1𝔸k1C^{\prime}\simeq\coprod_{i=1}^{m^{\prime}+1}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} of m′+1m^{\prime}+1 affine curves isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}. The closure of CC is contained in the singular fibre F0F_{0} of ZP−a¯→ℙk1\overline{Z_{P-a}}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, which is a tree of smooth rational curves of self-intersection ≤−1\leq-1, being a SNC divisor. Hence, the closure of each component of CC is a smooth rational curve of self-intersection ≤−1\leq-1, which intersects the boundary into a component lying in F0F_{0}. A similar description holds for C′C^{\prime}.

The curves CC, C′C^{\prime} meet transversally the conic Γ\Gamma given by x​y=1xy=1 (because of the form of P⁡(0,x,y)−aP(0,x,y)-a and Q⁡(0,x,y)−aQ(0,x,y)-a). The surfaces HP−a¯,HQ−a¯\overline{H_{P-a}},\overline{H_{Q-a}} are then obtained by blowing-up some points in each of the components of CC, C′C^{\prime} and removing these components, so we can choose the a minimal projectivisations of HP−a,HQ−aH_{P-a},H_{Q-a} to be blowing-ups of the above points in ZP−a¯,ZQ−a¯\overline{Z_{P-a}},\overline{Z_{Q-a}} and get a dual graph of the boundary of these surfaces which is not a chain (or which is not “linear” or not a “zigzag”). This implies that the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-fibration given by the tt-projection is unique up to automorphisms of the target ([Ber83, Theorème 1.8]). As the zero fibre of HP−a,HQ−a→𝔸k1H_{P-a},H_{Q-a}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is the unique degenerate fibre, there exist μa∈k∗\mu_{a}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and qa∈k​[t,u,x,y]q_{a}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y] such that φ∗​(t)=μa​t+qa⋅(P−a)\varphi^{*}(t)=\mu_{a}t+q_{a}\cdot(P-a). Since this holds for a general aa, we get φ∗​(t)=μ​t\varphi^{*}(t)=\mu t for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. Indeed, replacing tt with 00 in φ∗​(t)\varphi^{*}(t) yields an element of k​[u,x,y]/(x​y−1)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[u,x,y]/(xy-1) which is divisible by P−aP-a for infinitely many aa. This element is thus equal to zero.

We now show how Assertion (1) implies the two others. We write φ=φ1​φ2\varphi=\varphi_{1}\varphi_{2} where (φ1)∗​(t)=t(\varphi_{1})^{*}(t)=t and φ2\varphi_{2} is given by

Lemma 5.6 and Proposition 5.8 yield then the following result, which yields in particular Assertion (2) of Theorem 3:

Corollary 5.9.

If P,Q∈k​[t,x,y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] are polynomials which are variables of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y] and if the corresponding hypersurfaces HP,HQ⊂SL2=Spec⁡(k​[t,u,x,y]/(x​y−t​u−1))H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,u,x,y]/(xy-tu-1)) are equivalent and isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, the following hold:

  2. (2)(2)

    There exists φ∈Aut⁡(SL2)\varphi\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) such that φ⁡(HP)=HQ\varphi(H_{P})=H_{Q} and φ∗​(t)=μ​t\varphi^{*}(t)=\mu t for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. In particular, the element ψ=η​φ​η−1∈Aut⁡(𝔸k3)\psi=\eta\varphi\eta^{-1}\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) satisfies ψ∗​(t)=μ​t\psi^{*}(t)=\mu t, ψ⁡(ZP)=ZQ\psi(Z_{P})=Z_{Q} and ψ⁡(Γ)=Γ\psi(\Gamma)=\Gamma, where η:SL2→𝔸k3\eta\colon\SL_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is the morphism (t,u,x,y)↦(t,x,y)(t,u,x,y)\mapsto(t,x,y), ZP,ZQ⊂𝔸k3Z_{P},Z_{Q}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} are the two hypersurfaces given by P=0P=0, Q=0Q=0 and Γ⊂𝔸k3\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is the conic given by t=x​y−1=0t=xy-1=0.

Proof.

Assertion (1) follows from Proposition 5.4. It remains then to show (2). We denote by φ0∈Aut⁡(SL2)\varphi_{0}\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) an element such that φ0​(HP)=HQ\varphi_{0}(H_{P})=H_{Q}.

to obtain (φ0​θ)∗​(t)=t(\varphi_{0}\theta)^{*}(t)=t. 5.3. Examples of non-equivalent embeddings

Lemma 5.10.

To each polynomial r∈k​[t]r\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], we associate the polynomial

Pr=t​y−(x−t)​(x−1−t2​r​(t))∈k​[t,x,y]P_{r}=ty-(x-t)(x-1-t^{2}r(t))\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y]

    For each r,s∈k​[t]r,s\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], the following are equivalent

    3. (i​i​i)(iii)

      r=sr=s.

Proof.

For each r∈k​[t]r\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], we write Sr​(t,x)=(x−t)​(x−1−t2​r​(t))∈k​[t,x]S_{r}(t,x)=(x-t)(x-1-t^{2}r(t))\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x] and observe that Pr​(t,x,y)=t​y−Sr​(t,x)P_{r}(t,x,y)=ty-S_{r}(t,x).

(1): Since PrP_{r} is of degree 11 in yy, it is a variable of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]. Moreover, Pr​(0,x,y)=Sr​(0,x)=x⁡(x−1)P_{r}(0,x,y)=S_{r}(0,x)=x(x-1) is of the form μ​xm​(x−λ)\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda) (with μ,λ∈k∗\mu,\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and m≥0m\geq 0). The coefficient of yy in PrP_{r} being tt, the morphism ZPr→𝔸k1Z_{P_{r}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, (t,x,y)↦t(t,x,y)\mapsto t is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle over 𝔸k1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\{0\}. Proposition 5.4 ((c)⇒(b)\eqref{ThmEqc}\Rightarrow\eqref{ThmEqb}) then implies that HPr⊂SL2H_{P_{r}}\subset\SL_{2} is the image of a fibred embedding 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}.

It remains to show that the assertions (2i)−(2ii)−(2iii)−(2iv)(\ref{EquivRSHeq})-(\ref{EquivRSZeq})-(\ref{EquivRSZiso})-(\ref{EquivRSequal}) of (2)(\ref{EquivRS}) are equivalent.

The implications (2iv)⇒(2i)(\ref{EquivRSequal})\Rightarrow(\ref{EquivRSHeq}) and (2ii)⇒(2iii)(\ref{EquivRSZeq})\Rightarrow(\ref{EquivRSZiso}) are trivial.

Lemma 5.6 implies that ZPrZ_{P_{r}} and ZPsZ_{P_{s}} are not isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} (the integer mm being here equal to 11). We can thus appply Proposition 5.8(2), which yields (2i)⇒(2ii)(\ref{EquivRSHeq})\Rightarrow(\ref{EquivRSZeq}).

It remains then to show (2iii)⇒(2iv)(\ref{EquivRSZiso})\Rightarrow(\ref{EquivRSequal}). According to [DP09, Proposition 3.6], the surface ZPrZ_{P_{r}} and ZPsZ_{P_{s}} are isomorphic if and only if there exist a,μ∈k∗a,\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast}, τ∈k​[t]\tau\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], such that

Sr​(a​t,x)=μ2​Ss​(t,μ−1​x+τ⁡(t))inside k​[t,x].S_{r}(at,x)=\mu^{2}S_{s}(t,\mu^{-1}x+\tau(t))\quad\textrm{inside $\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x]$}.

This corresponds to

(x−a​t)​(x−1−a2​t2​r​(a​t))=(x+μ⁡(τ⁡(t)−t))​(x+μ⁡(τ⁡(t)−1−t2​s​(t)))(x-at)(x-1-a^{2}t^{2}r(at))=(x+\mu(\tau(t)-t))(x+\mu(\tau(t)-1-t^{2}s(t)))

and thus gives two possibilities:

(I)(\mathrm{I}): a​t=μ⁡(t−τ⁡(t))at=\mu(t-\tau(t)) and 1+a2​t2​r​(a​t)=μ⁡(1+t2​s​(t)−τ⁡(t))1+a^{2}t^{2}r(at)=\mu(1+t^{2}s(t)-\tau(t)). The first equation yields τ⁡(t)=(1−aμ)​t\tau(t)=(1-\frac{a}{\mu})t and the second yields μ​τ​(t)≡μ−1(modt2)\mu\tau(t)\equiv\mu-1\pmod{t^{2}}, which gives τ=0\tau=0 and then μ=1\mu=1 and a=1a=1. The second equation thus yields r⁡(t)=s⁡(t)r(t)=s(t).

(II)(\mathrm{II}): a​t=μ⁡(1+t2​s​(t)−τ⁡(t))at=\mu(1+t^{2}s(t)-\tau(t)) and μ⁡(t−τ⁡(t))=1+a2​t2​r​(a​t)\mu(t-\tau(t))=1+a^{2}t^{2}r(at). This yields

1+a2​t2​r​(a​t)−μ​t=−μ​τ​(t)=a​t−μ⁡(1+t2​s​(t))1+a^{2}t^{2}r(at)-\mu t=-\mu\tau(t)=at-\mu(1+t^{2}s(t))

and thus 1−μ​t≡−μ+a​t(modt2)1-\mu t\equiv-\mu+at\pmod{t^{2}}, whence μ=−1\mu=-1 and a=1a=1. Replacing in the equation above, we find r⁡(t)=s⁡(t)r(t)=s(t). ∎

The proof of Theorem 3 is now clear:

Proof of Theorem 3.

Assertion (1) corresponds to Proposition 5.4.

Assertion (2) follows from Corollary 5.9.

Assertion (3) follows from Lemma 5.10, which yields hypersurfaces HPr⊂SL2H_{P_{r}}\subset\SL_{2} that are parametrised by r∈k​[t]r\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], which are all images of fibred embeddings and are pairwise non-equivalent. ∎

We finish this subsection with two explicit examples:

Lemma 5.11.

Let us denote by P,Q∈k​[t,x,y]P,Q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,x,y] the polynomials

P=t2​y−x⁡(x+1)andQ=t2​y−x⁡(x+1−t2).P=t^{2}y-x(x+1)\quad\textrm{and}\quad Q=t^{2}y-x(x+1-t^{2})\,.

Then, the following hold:

  1. (1)(1)

    The hypersurfaces ZP,ZQ⊂𝔸k3Z_{P},Z_{Q}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by P=0P=0 and Q=0Q=0 are equivalent.

  2. (2)(2)

    The hypersurfaces HP,HQ⊂SL2H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2} given by P=0P=0 and Q=0Q=0 are both images of fibred embeddings but are not equivalent.

Proof.

To get (1), it suffices to observe that the linear automorphism θ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k3)\theta\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) given by (t,x,y)↦(t,x,y−x)(t,x,y)\mapsto(t,x,y-x) satisfies θ∗​(Q)=P\theta^{*}(Q)=P, so θ⁡(ZP)=ZQ\theta(Z_{P})=Z_{Q}.

Since P,QP,Q are of degree 11 in yy, both are variables of the k​(t)\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)-algebra k​(t)​[x,y]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}(t)[x,y]. Moreover, P⁡(0,x,y)=Q⁡(0,x,y)=−x⁡(x+1)P(0,x,y)=Q(0,x,y)=-x(x+1) is of the form μ​xm​(x−λ)\mu x^{m}(x-\lambda) (with μ,λ∈k∗\mu,\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and m=1≥0m=1\geq 0). Since the coefficient of yy in PP and QQ is t2t^{2}, the morphisms ZP,ZQ→𝔸k1Z_{P},Z_{Q}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}, (t,x,y)↦t(t,x,y)\mapsto t are trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundles over 𝔸k1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}. Proposition 5.4 ((c)⇒(b)\eqref{ThmEqc}\Rightarrow\eqref{ThmEqb}) then implies that HP,HQ⊂SL2H_{P},H_{Q}\subset\SL_{2} are images of fibred embeddings 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}.

To get (2), we suppose that there is φ∈Aut⁡(SL2)\varphi\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) such that φ⁡(HP)=HQ\varphi(H_{P})=H_{Q} and derive a contradiction. Corollary 5.9 yields an automorphism ψ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k3)\psi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) such that ψ∗​(t)=μ​t\psi^{*}(t)=\mu t for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and such that ψ⁡(ZP)=ZQ\psi(Z_{P})=Z_{Q} and ψ⁡(Γ)=Γ\psi(\Gamma)=\Gamma, where Γ⊂𝔸k3\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} is the conic given by t=x​y−1=0t=xy-1=0. The restriction of ψ\psi to the hyperplane H⊂𝔸k3H\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} given by t=0t=0 then preserves Γ\Gamma and also the curve C=H∩ZP=H∩ZQC=H\cap Z_{P}=H\cap Z_{Q}, given by t=x⁡(x+1)=0t=x(x+1)=0 (which is isomorphic to two copies of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}). The fact that CC is preserved implies that ψ|H\psi_{|_{H}} is of the form (x,y)↦(x,a​y+p⁡(x))(x,y)\mapsto(x,ay+p(x)) or (x,y)↦(−1−x,a​y+p⁡(x))(x,y)\mapsto(-1-x,ay+p(x)) for some a∈k∗a\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and p∈k​[x]p\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[x]. The fact that Γ\Gamma is preserved implies that ψ|H=id\psi_{|_{H}}=\mathrm{id}.

The element ξ=θ−1​ψ∈Aut⁡(𝔸k3)\xi=\theta^{-1}\psi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}) then satisfies ξ⁡(ZP)=ZP\xi(Z_{P})=Z_{P}, ξ∗​(t)=μ​t\xi^{*}(t)=\mu t and ξ|H\xi_{|_{H}} is the automorphism (x,y)↦(x,x+y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,x+y). To show that this is impossible, we use [DP09, Theorem 3.11] to see that every automorphism of ZPZ_{P} preserves CC and its action on CC corresponds to an element of the subgroup G=G0∪G1≃G0⋊(ℤ/2​ℤ)G=G_{0}\cup G_{1}\simeq G_{0}\rtimes({\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}) of Aut⁡(C)\Aut(C) given by

Question 5.13.

Is the closed embedding
