equivalent to the standard one?

5.4. Embeddings of 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}} into SL2\SL_{2} of small degree

This last subsection consists in showing the second part of Remark 1.1, which claims that if all component functions of a closed embedding f:𝔸2↪SL2f\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} are polynomials of degree ≤2\leq 2, then ff is equivalent to ρλ\rho_{\lambda} for a certain λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast}. This will be done in Proposition 5.19 below, after a few lemmas.

We first make the following easy observation:

Lemma 5.14.

For each fibred embedding

ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(a⁡(s,t)tc⁡(s,t)b⁡(s,t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}a(s,t)&t\\ c(s,t)&b(s,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

((with 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁a,b,c∈k​[s,t])a,b,c\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t]) there is an automorphism g∈Aut⁡(SL2)g\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) such that g​ρg\rho is a fibred embedding given by

g​ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(1+s​t​p​(s,t)ts⁡(p⁡(s,t)+q⁡(s,t)+s​t​p​(s,t)​q​(s,t))1+s​t​q​(s,t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}g\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1+stp(s,t)&t\\ s(p(s,t)+q(s,t)+stp(s,t)q(s,t))&1+stq(s,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

for some p,q∈k​[s,t]p,q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] such that p⁡(s,0)+q⁡(s,0)∈k∗p(s,0)+q(s,0)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and such that deg⁡(1+s​t​p​(s,t))≤deg⁡(a)\deg(1+stp(s,t))\leq\deg(a), deg⁡(1+s​t​q​(s,t))≤deg⁡(b)\deg(1+stq(s,t))\leq\deg(b) ((where the degree is here the degree of polynomials in 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁s,t)s,t).

Remark 5.15.

The standard embedding ρ1\rho_{1} is of the above form with p=0p=0 and q=1q=1. More generally, the embeddings {ρλ}λ∈k∗\{\rho_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}} of Theorem 2 are given by p=0p=0 and q=λq=\lambda.

Proof.

Replacing tt with 00 yields two elements a⁡(s,0),b⁡(s,0)∈k​[s]a(s,0),b(s,0)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s] such that a⁡(s,0)⋅b⁡(s,0)=1a(s,0)\cdot b(s,0)=1. This implies that a⁡(s,0),b⁡(s,0)∈k∗a(s,0),b(s,0)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. Applying the automorphism

(xtuy)↦(μ​xtuμ−1​y)\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\mu x&t\\ u&\mu^{-1}y\end{pmatrix}

for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}, we can assume that a⁡(s,0)=b⁡(s,0)=1a(s,0)=b(s,0)=1. We then apply

(xtuy)↦(xtuy)⋅(10d⁡(t)1)\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ d(t)&1\end{pmatrix}

for some d∈k​[t]d\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] and replace a⁡(s,t)a(s,t) with a⁡(s,t)+t​d​(t)a(s,t)+td(t), so can assume that a⁡(0,t)=1a(0,t)=1. Applying similarly an automorphism of the form

(xtuy)↦(10e⁡(t)1)⋅(xtuy),\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ e(t)&1\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix},

we can assume that b⁡(0,t)=1b(0,t)=1. This yields p,q∈k​[s,t]p,q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] such that a=1+s​t​pa=1+stp and b=1+s​t​qb=1+stq, which yields c=s⁡(p+q+s​t​p​q)c=s(p+q+stpq). Replacing tt with 00 yields a closed embedding

𝔸k1↪SL2s↦(10s⁡(p⁡(s,0)+q⁡(s,0))1),\begin{array}[]{cccc}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ s&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ s(p(s,0)+q(s,0))&1\end{pmatrix}\end{array},

whence p⁡(s,0)+q⁡(s,0)∈k∗p(s,0)+q(s,0)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. ∎

Corollary 5.16.

Each fibred embedding

ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(a⁡(s,t)tc⁡(s,t)b⁡(s,t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}a(s,t)&t\\ c(s,t)&b(s,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

where a,b,c∈k​[s,t]a,b,c\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] are such that deg⁡a+deg⁡b≤4\deg a+\deg b\leq 4 is equivalent to the embedding

ρλ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(1tλ​s1+λ​s​t)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{\lambda}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\ \lambda s&1+\lambda st\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

for some λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}.

Proof.

Applying Lemma 5.14, one can assume that a=1+s​t​pa=1+stp, b=1+s​t​qb=1+stq, c=s⁡(p+q+s​t​p​q)c=s(p+q+stpq) for some p,q∈k​[s,t]p,q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] with p⁡(s,0)+q⁡(s,0)∈k∗p(s,0)+q(s,0)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. If p=0p=0, then ρ⁡(𝔸2)\rho({\mathbb{A}}^{2}) is equal to ρ1​(𝔸2)\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}), so the result follows from Theorem 2(1). The same holds if q=0q=0 by applying the automorphism

(xtuy)↦(ytux).\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}y&t\\ u&x\end{pmatrix}.

To finish the proof, we assume that p​q≠0pq\not=0 and derive a contradiction. The fact that deg⁡a+deg⁡b≤4\deg a+\deg b\leq 4 implies that p,q∈k∗p,q\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. Hence, k​[s,t]=k​[a,b,c,t]=k​[t,s​t,s⁡(p+q+s​t​p​q)]=k​[t,s​t,s⁡(s​t+ξ)]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[a,b,c,t]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,st,s(p+q+stpq)]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t,st,s(st+\xi)] with ξ=p+qp​q≠0\xi=\frac{p+q}{pq}\neq 0, and thus the morphism

𝔸k2↦𝔸k3(s,t)↦(t,s​t,s⁡(s​t+ξ))\begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\mapsto&{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\\ (s,t)&\mapsto&(t,st,s(st+\xi))\end{array}

would be a closed embedding. This is false, since the image is properly contained in the irreducible hypersurface given by {(x,y,z)∈𝔸k3∣x​z=y⁡(y+ξ)}\{(x,y,z)\in{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\mid xz=y(y+\xi)\} (the line given by x=y+ξ=0x=y+\xi=0 is missing). ∎

It remains to generalise Corollary 5.16 to the case of embeddings 𝔸k2↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} of small degree (which are fibred or not).

In the sequel we will use the following subgroups of Aut⁡(𝔸k2)\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}):

Definition 5.17.
Aff2⁡(k)={(s,t)↦(as+bt+e,cs+dt+f)|(abcd)∈GL2(k),e,f∈k}GL2⁡(k)={(s,t)↦(as+bt,cs+dt)|a,b,c,d∈k,ad−bc≠0}\begin{array}[]{lll}\Aff_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})&=&\left\{(s,t)\mapsto(as+bt+e,cs+dt+f)\left|\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\GL_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}),e,f\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}\right\}\right.\\ \GL_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}})&=&\left\{(s,t)\mapsto(as+bt,cs+dt)\left|a,b,c,d\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}},\ ad-bc\neq 0\right\}\right.\end{array}
Lemma 5.18.

Let k be an algebraically closed field and let ρ:𝔸k2→𝔸k2∖{0}\rho\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\{0\} be a morphism of the form

(s,t)↦(f⁡(s,t),g⁡(s,t))(s,t)\mapsto(f(s,t),g(s,t))

such that f,gf,g have degree 22 and that the homogeneous parts f2f_{2} and g2g_{2} of f,gf,g of degree 22 are linearly independent. Then, there exist α∈Aff2\alpha\in\Aff_{2} and β∈GL2\beta\in\GL_{2} such that

β​ρ​α=(s,t)↦(s2,s​t+1).\beta\rho\alpha=(s,t)\mapsto(s^{2},st+1).
Proof.

We first observe that replacing ρ\rho with β​ρ​α\beta\rho\alpha, where α∈Aff2\alpha\in\Aff_{2} and β∈GL2\beta\in\GL_{2}, does not change the degree of f,gf,g or the fact that f2f_{2} and g2g_{2} are linearly independent. We then observe that we can assume that f2=s2f_{2}=s^{2}. If f2f_{2} is a square, it suffices to replace ff with ρ​α\rho\alpha for some α∈GL2\alpha\in\GL_{2}. If f2f_{2} is not a square, we choose ξ∈k\xi\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}} such that g2+ξ​f2g_{2}+\xi f_{2} is a square (this is possible since the discriminant of g2+ξ​f2g_{2}+\xi f_{2} is a polynomial of degree 22 in ξ\xi and k is algebraically closed). We then apply an element of GL2\GL_{2} at the target to replace f2,g2f_{2},g_{2} with g2+ξ​f2,f2g_{2}+\xi f_{2},f_{2},and then apply as before an element of GL2\GL_{2} at the source, to obtain f2=s2f_{2}=s^{2}.

For each irreducible factor PP of ff, we denote by CP⊂𝔸k2=Spec⁡(k​[s,t])C_{P}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}=\Spec(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t]) the irreducible curve given by P=0P=0, and observe that gg yields an invertible function on CPC_{P}.

(a)(a) If ff is a product of factors of degree 11, all belong to k​[s]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s], since f2=s2f_{2}=s^{2}. We can then write f=∏i=12(s−λi)f=\prod_{i=1}^{2}(s-\lambda_{i}), for some λi∈k\lambda_{i}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}. If λ1=λ2\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}, we replace ss with s−λ1s-\lambda_{1} and get f=s2f=s^{2}, which yields g=s⁡(a​s+b​t+c)+dg=s(as+bt+c)+d for some a,b,c∈k,d∈k∗a,b,c\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}},d\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}. The parts of degree 22 of ff and gg being linearly independent, we get b≠0b\not=0. Replacing tt with t−a​s−cb\frac{t-as-c}{b}, we replace gg with s​t+dst+d. We then apply diagonal elements of the form (s,t)↦(s,μ​t)(s,t)\mapsto(s,\mu t), μ∈k∗\mu\in k^{\ast} at the source and target and replace dd with 11, which yields the desired form. To finish case (a)(a), it remains to see that λ1≠λ2\lambda_{1}\neq\lambda_{2} is impossible. This implies that the restriction g|Cfg|_{C_{f}} is a non-zero constant and so g=μ+ξ​fg=\mu+\xi f for some μ∈k∗,ξ∈k\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{\ast},\xi\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}. Proposition 5.19.

Each closed embedding

ρ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(f11​(s,t)f12​(s,t)f21​(s,t)f22​(s,t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}f_{11}(s,t)&f_{12}(s,t)\\ f_{21}(s,t)&f_{22}(s,t)\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

where f11,f12,f21,f22∈k​[s,t]f_{11},f_{12},f_{21},f_{22}\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] have at most degree 22 is equivalent to the embedding

ρλ:𝔸k2↪SL2(s,t)↦(1tλ​s1+λ​s​t)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\rho_{\lambda}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &(s,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\ \lambda s&1+\lambda st\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

for some λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*}.

Proof.

Applying Theorem 2, one only needs to show the existence of an automorphism of SL2\SL_{2} that sends ρ⁡(𝔸k2)\rho({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}) onto ρ1​(𝔸k2)\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}^{2}). We distinguish the following cases:

(a)(a) Suppose first that one of the polynomials fi​jf_{ij} is constant. One can assume that it is f11f_{11} by using permutation of coordinates (with signs). The case f11=0f_{11}=0 is impossible, since the image would then be contained in

{(xtuy)∈SL2|x=0}≃(𝔸k1∖{0})×𝔸k1.\left.\left\{\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\in\SL_{2}\right|x=0\right\}\simeq({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\{0\})\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}.

We then have f11≠0f_{11}\not=0 and apply a diagonal automorphism of SL2\SL_{2} to get f11=1f_{11}=1, which corresponds to ρ⁡(𝔸k2)=ρ1​(𝔸k2)\rho({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}})=\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}).

(b)(b) Suppose then that one of the fi​jf_{ij} has degree 11. Applying permutations one can assume that f12f_{12} has degree 11. Applying an element of Aff2\Aff_{2} at the source (see Definition 5.17), we do not change the degree of the fi​j′​s{f_{ij}}^{\prime}s and can assume that f12=tf_{12}=t. Since deg⁡(f11​f22)=deg⁡(f12​f21)≤4\deg(f_{11}f_{22})=\deg(f_{12}f_{21})\leq 4, the result follows from Corollary 5.16.

(c)(c) It remains to study the case where deg⁡(fi​j)=2\deg(f_{ij})=2 for each i,j∈{1,2}i,j\in\{1,2\}. If the homogeneous parts of f11f_{11} and f12f_{12} of degree 22 are collinear, we apply

(xtuy)↦(xtuy)​(1μ01)=(xt+μ​xuy+μ​u)\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&\mu\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x&t+\mu x\\ u&y+\mu u\end{pmatrix}

for some μ∈k\mu\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}} and obtain deg⁡(f12)≤1\deg(f_{12})\leq 1, which reduces to the cases (a)(a), (b)(b). To achieve the proof of (c)(c), we now assume that the homogeneous parts of f11f_{11} and f12f_{12} of degree 22 are linearly independant and prove that this implies that k​[f11,f12,f21,f22]⊊k​[s,t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[f_{11},f_{12},f_{21},f_{22}]\subsetneq\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t] (which contradicts the fact that ρ\rho is a closed embedding). To show this, one can extend the scalars and assume that k is algebraically closed. We then apply Lemma 5.18 to the morphism ν:𝔸k2→𝔸k2∖{0}\nu\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{\mathbf{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\{0\} given by (s,t)↦(f11​(s,t),f12​(s,t))(s,t)\mapsto(f_{11}(s,t),f_{12}(s,t)), and find α∈Aff2⁡(k)\alpha\in\Aff_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}), β∈GL2⁡(k)\beta\in\GL_{2}(\mathbf{\textbf{k}}) such that β​ν​α=(s,t)↦(s2,s​t+1)\beta\nu\alpha=(s,t)\mapsto(s^{2},st+1). We write μ=det(β)∈k∗\mu=\det(\beta)\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}^{*} and replace ρ\rho with β^​ρ​α\hat{\beta}\rho\alpha, where β^∈Aut⁡(SL2)\hat{\beta}\in\Aut(\SL_{2}) is of the form

β^:(xtuy)↦(100μ−1)⋅β⋅(xtuy).\hat{\beta}\colon\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\mu^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\cdot\beta\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}.

This implies that f11,f12−1,f21+1f_{11},f_{12}-1,f_{21}+1 all belong to the maximal ideal (s,t)2⊂k​[s,t](s,t)^{2}\subset\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t], which yields the desired contradiction k​[f11,f12,f21,f22]=k​[f11,f12−1,f21+1,f22]⊊k​[s,t]\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[f_{11},f_{12},f_{21},f_{22}]=\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[f_{11},f_{12}-1,f_{21}+1,f_{22}]\subsetneq\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[s,t]. ∎

6. A non-trivial embedding of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} into SL2\SL_{2}, over the reals

In this section, we provide over the field k=ℝ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}={\mathbb{R}} an explicit example of an algebraic embedding 𝔸ℝ1↪SL2{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{R}}}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2} which is not equivalent to the standard embedding

τ1:𝔸ℝ1↪SL2t↦(10t1).\begin{array}[]{cccc}\tau_{1}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{\mathbb{R}}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &t&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ t&1\end{pmatrix}\,.\end{array}
Example 6.1.

In [Sha92] the closed embedding

γ:𝔸1↪𝔸3t↦(t3−3​t,t4−4​t2−1,t5−10​t)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\gamma\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}&\hookrightarrow&{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\\ &t&\mapsto&(t^{3}-3t,t^{4}-4t^{2}-1,t^{5}-10t)\end{array}

is given. This one is not equivalent to the standard embedding 𝔸1↪𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{3}, t↦(t,0,0)t\mapsto(t,0,0), over the field ℝ{\mathbb{R}} of real numbers. The reason is that it corresponds, as an embedding ℝ↪ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, to the (open) trefoil knot.

The fact that γ\gamma is a closed embedding, over any field k, can be shown as follows. Writing γ1=t3−3​t,γ2=t4−4​t2−1,γ3=t5−10​t∈k​[t]\gamma_{1}=t^{3}-3t,\gamma_{2}=t^{4}-4t^{2}-1,\gamma_{3}=t^{5}-10t\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t], we get

t=3​γ3−12​γ1−5​γ1​γ2+γ2​γ3−γ13.t=3\gamma_{3}-12\gamma_{1}-5\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}-\gamma_{1}^{3}.

The fact that γ:ℝ→ℝ3\gamma\colon{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{3} corresponds to the open trefoil knot can be seen by looking at the three projections:

We now use Example 6.1 to provide a similar example in SL2\SL_{2}:

Lemma 6.2.
  1. (1)(1)

    For each field k of characteristic ≠2\not=2, the morphism

    τ:𝔸1↪SL2t↦(t3−3​tt4−4​t2−11+t2​(17​t6−56​t4−137​t2+452)16t⁡(17​t8−73​t6−149​t4+609​t2+172)16)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\tau\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &t&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}t^{3}-3t&t^{4}-4t^{2}-1\\ 1+\frac{t^{2}(17t^{6}-56t^{4}-137t^{2}+452)}{16}&\frac{t(17t^{8}-73t^{6}-149t^{4}+609t^{2}+172)}{16}\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

    is a closed embedding.

  2. (2)(2)

    If k=ℝ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}={\mathbb{R}}, then τ\tau is not equivalent to the standard embedding, because the fundamental group π1​(SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ⁡(ℝ))\pi_{1}(\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})) is not isomorphic to the free group π1​(SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ1​(ℝ))\pi_{1}(\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau_{1}({\mathbb{R}})).

Proof.

(1): The fact that τ\tau is a closed embedding can be done explicitely by giving a formula for tt, but can also be shown by using the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle

p:SL2→𝔸2∖{(0,0)}(xtuy)↦(x,t).\begin{array}[]{cccc}p\colon&\SL_{2}&\to&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\\ &\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ u&y\end{pmatrix}&\mapsto&(x,t).\end{array}

Writing γ1=t3−3​t,γ2=t4−4​t2−1,γ3=t5−10​t∈k​[t]\gamma_{1}=t^{3}-3t,\gamma_{2}=t^{4}-4t^{2}-1,\gamma_{3}=t^{5}-10t\in\mathbf{\textbf{k}}[t] as in Example 6.1, we get γ12​(γ12−4)−γ2​(γ22+9​γ2+24)=16\gamma_{1}^{2}(\gamma_{1}^{2}-4)-\gamma_{2}(\gamma_{2}^{2}+9\gamma_{2}+24)=16 and thus get a birational morphism

𝔸1→Γ={(x,t)∈𝔸2∣x2​(x2−4)−t⁡(t2+9​t+24)=16}t↦(γ1​(t),γ2​(t))\begin{array}[]{ccc}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}&\to&\Gamma=\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\mid x^{2}(x^{2}-4)-t(t^{2}+9t+24)=16\}\\ t&\mapsto&(\gamma_{1}(t),\gamma_{2}(t))\end{array}

from 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} to the singular affine quartic curve Γ⊂𝔸2\Gamma\subset\lx@nobreakspace{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. We then get a morphism

f:Γ→SL2(x,t)→(xtt2+9​t+2416x⁡(x2−4)16)\begin{array}[]{rccc}f\colon&\Gamma&\to&\SL_{2}\\ &(x,t)&\to&\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ \frac{t^{2}+9t+24}{16}&\frac{x(x^{2}-4)}{16}\end{pmatrix}\end{array}

which satisfies p∘f=idΓp\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{\Gamma} and is thus a section of pp over Γ\Gamma. This implies that

Γ×𝔸1↪SL2((x,t),a)↦(10a1)​f​(x,t)\begin{array}[]{ccc}\Gamma\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ ((x,t),a)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ a&1\end{pmatrix}f(x,t)\end{array}

is a closed embedding. Since γ:𝔸1→Γ×𝔸1⊂𝔸3\gamma\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to\Gamma\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{3} is a closed embedding, the morphism

τ:𝔸1↪SL2t↦(10t5−10​t1)​f​(γ1​(t),γ2​(t))\begin{array}[]{cccc}\tau\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{1}&\hookrightarrow&\SL_{2}\\ &t&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ t^{5}-10t&1\end{pmatrix}f(\gamma_{1}(t),\gamma_{2}(t))\end{array}

is a closed embedding. Replacing γ1\gamma_{1} and γ2\gamma_{2} in the above formula yields the explicit form of the morphism given in the statement of the lemma.

(2): In the remaining part of the proof, we work over k=ℝ\mathbf{\textbf{k}}={\mathbb{R}} and use the Euclidean topology. The ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-bundle p:SL2⁡(ℝ)→ℝ2∖{(0,0)}p\colon\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\to{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\} is trivial, as it admits a (rational) continuous section given by

ξ:ℝ2∖{(0,0)}→SL2⁡(ℝ)(x,t)↦(xt−tx2+t2xx2+t2).\begin{array}[]{cccc}\xi\colon&{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}&\to&\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\\ &(x,t)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}x&t\\ -\frac{t}{x^{2}+t^{2}}&\frac{x}{x^{2}+t^{2}}\end{pmatrix}.\end{array}

This yields a birational diffeomorphism

φ:ℝ2∖{(0,0)}×ℝ→SL2⁡(ℝ)((x,t),a)↦(10a1)​ξ​(x,t).\begin{array}[]{cccc}\varphi\colon&{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\times{\mathbb{R}}&\to&\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\\ &((x,t),a)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ a&1\end{pmatrix}\xi(x,t)\,.\end{array}

In particular, SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ1​(ℝ)\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau_{1}({\mathbb{R}}) is diffeomorphic to ℝ2∖{(0,0),(0,1)}×ℝ{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0),(0,1)\}\times{\mathbb{R}}, which implies that the fundamental group π1​(SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ1​(ℝ))\pi_{1}(\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau_{1}({\mathbb{R}})) is a free group (over two generators). It remains to show that π1​(SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ⁡(ℝ))\pi_{1}(\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})) is not a free group. This will imply that no diffeomorphism of SL2⁡(ℝ)\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) sends τ⁡(ℝ)\tau({\mathbb{R}}) onto τ1​(ℝ)\tau_{1}({\mathbb{R}}), and in particular no algebraic automorphism defined over ℝ{\mathbb{R}}.

We extend f:Γ⁡(ℝ)→SL2⁡(ℝ)f\colon\Gamma({\mathbb{R}})\to\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) to a global continuous section f^:ℝ2∖{(0,0)}→SL2⁡(ℝ)\hat{f}\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\to\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}}) of pp (which exists, since pp is a trivial ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-bundle). This yields a rational diffeomorphism

g:ℝ2∖{(0,0)}×ℝ⟶≃SL2⁡(ℝ)((x,t),a)↦(10a1)​f^​(x,t)\begin{array}[]{ccc}g\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\}\times{\mathbb{R}}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\\ ((x,t),a)&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ a&1\end{pmatrix}\hat{f}(x,t)\end{array}

which maps γ⁡(ℝ)\gamma({\mathbb{R}}) onto τ⁡(ℝ)\tau({\mathbb{R}}).

We take an open subset U⊂ℝ2∖{(0,0)}U\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\} (for the Euclidean topology) that contains the singular curve Γ⁡(ℝ)\Gamma({\mathbb{R}}) and a homeomorphism h:U⟶≃ℝ2h\colon U\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{R}}^{2} which fixes Γ⁡(ℝ)\Gamma({\mathbb{R}}) pointwise, and which is homotopic to the inclusion U↪ℝ2U\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, via a homotopy that fixes Γ⁡(ℝ)\Gamma({\mathbb{R}}) pointwise. We can for instance take U={(x,t)∈ℝ2∣t≤x2−12}U=\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\mid t\leq x^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\} and construct a homeomorphism and a homotopy which preserve the fibres of the projection (x,t)↦x(x,t)\mapsto x.

The homeomorphisms

(⋆\star) p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ)⟶g−1(U×ℝ)∖γ⁡(ℝ)⟶h×idℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ)p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g^{-1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\left(U\times{\mathbb{R}}\right)\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h\times\mathrm{id}}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})

yield isomorphisms of the fundamental groups

π1​(p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ))⟶≃π1​((U×ℝ)∖γ⁡(ℝ))⟶≃π1​(ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ)).\pi_{1}(p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}\pi_{1}((U\times{\mathbb{R}})\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}}))\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}\pi_{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}}))\,.

Since γ:ℝ↪ℝ3\gamma\colon{\mathbb{R}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is the (open) trefoil knot, it follows that π1​(ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ))\pi_{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})) is the braid group with 33 strands and thus π1​(p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ))\pi_{1}(p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})) is not a free group. It remains then to see that the group homomorphism

ι:π1​(p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ))→π1​(SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ⁡(ℝ))\iota\colon\pi_{1}(p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}}))\to\pi_{1}(\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}}))

induced by the inclusion p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ)↪SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ⁡(ℝ)p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}}) is injective (as a subgroup of a free group is free). Every element α∈Ker⁡(ι)\alpha\in\mathrm{Ker}(\iota) lies in the kernel of the map ι′:π1​(p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ))→π1​(ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ))\iota^{\prime}\colon\pi_{1}(p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}}))\to\pi_{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})) induced by the composition

p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ)↪SL2⁡(ℝ)∖τ⁡(ℝ)⟶g−1((ℝ2∖{(0,0)})×ℝ)∖γ⁡(ℝ)↪ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ),p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}({\mathbb{R}})\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g^{-1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}(({\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus\{(0,0)\})\times{\mathbb{R}})\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}}),

which corresponds simply to the composition

(⋆⁣⋆\star\star) p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ)⟶g−1(U×ℝ)∖γ⁡(ℝ)↪ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ).p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g^{-1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\left(U\times{\mathbb{R}}\right)\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}})\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}}).

Since h:U→ℝ2h\colon U\to{\mathbb{R}}^{2} is homotopic to the inclusion U↪ℝ2U\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{2} via a homotopy that fixes Γ⁡(ℝ)\Gamma({\mathbb{R}}) pointwise, the two compositions p−1​(U)∖τ⁡(ℝ)→ℝ3∖γ⁡(ℝ)p^{-1}(U)\setminus\tau({\mathbb{R}})\to{\mathbb{R}}^{3}\setminus\gamma({\mathbb{R}}) of ( ⋆ ‣ 6) and ( ⋆ ⁣ ⋆ ‣ 6) are homotopic, so ι′\iota^{\prime} is an isomorphism. This implies that ι\iota is injective and achieves the proof. ∎

Question 6.3.

Working over the field of complex numbers ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, is the algebraic embedding τ:𝔸1→SL2\tau\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to\SL_{2} of Lemma 6.2(1) equivalent to the standard embedding τ1:𝔸1↪SL2\tau_{1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\hookrightarrow\SL_{2}?
